#6351. The Best Food Gifts Under $100 (That Are Just the Right Amount of Extra)

These luxe but affordable gifts feel sumptuous and whimsical, from eggnog petit fours to a glass ham ornament

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

I take my holiday gift shopping very seriously — if not for my giftee, for my own serotonin-seeking purposes. There’s nothing quite as satisfying as finding the right N/A cocktail bundle for your aunt, or a cake stand that doubles as a chip and dip bowl (the in-laws will love that one) for the avid entertainer.

We’re all on different budgets; some are on the hunt for tasty bargains and piggy-bank-friendly stocking stuffers, while others have a more robust chunk of change set aside for providing big-impact presents You might have already bookmarked Eater’s gift guides that are under-$25, which is full of all kinds of chic home and kitchen goods, but now [turns up gas] we’re shopping at the under-$100 range, which gives us even more wiggle room to sweep your giftees off their feet via a ham-themed ornament, a robust at-home chai kit, or a set of steak knives from Peter Luger.

We’re in prime gift guide season, folks. Fasten your aprons, and let’s shop for every kind of food-loving person on your holiday list.

No cocktail has been living, laughing, and loving harder than the ultra-dirty martini lately. This briny bundle from Big Night brings together the shoppy shop’s sleek olive-themed hors d’oeuvres picks with a jar of Quincy’s big, juicy Castelvetrano olives, Quincy cocktail onions, and bag of Filthy’s cult-fave olive brine.

For my money, a solid indicator of a fun household is whether or not there’s a wild cheese or cutting board in the mix. This psychedelic slab from Fredericks and Mae is both a beautiful serving board and functional chopping block for all of your kitchen needs, because it’s made out of a durable and non-toxic HDPE material.

Fredericks and Mae Red/Blue Cutting Board

The organic Los Angeles lifestyle brand Flamingo Estate has created the pasta-lover’s dream present: a chic trio of pomodoro rosso sauce, angel trumpet pasta, and a bottle of Flamingo Estate’s heritage EVOO. As with the rest of the Estate’s bundles, this set comes housed in one of its signature, ornate green boxes.

Imagine the flex of sawing through a Porterhouse at home with Peter Luger logo-stamped blades, which are made with stainless steel and wood handles that will transport their giftee back to the hallowed halls of the world-famous Brooklyn steakhouse. If you have a bit more room left in your gift budget, I suggest pairing it with some New York strip steaks from Snake River Farms.

Diaspora Spice Co. is one of Eater’s favorite places to buy spices online, because it’s home to dozens of single-origin heirloom spices from (mostly) India and Sri Lanka. As founder Sana Javeri Kadri explains on its site, a core tenant of Diaspora Spice Co.’s operations is rooted in undoing colonialist inequity in the spice trade; in her words: “We’re proud to pay our farm partners an average of 6x above the commodity price. In a system where fair trade is a mere 15 percent premium, we pay what we believe to be a living wage.” The equitable spice brand has partnered with the North Carolina-based pottery and lifestyle brand East Fork on this at-home chai bundle, which features the former’s brand new masala chai blend, Madhur jaggery, a stainless steel strainer, and a panna cotta colorway kuhlad from the indie pottery company.

Eater’s deputy brand director Nat Belkov introduced me to Craighill, a company that reimagines everyday carry and home essentials (think, scissors and carabiners) with a little more design flair. The Brooklyn-based studio redesigned the common wine key, and Belkov tells me that it mitigates all the annoying little things that can go wrong while using a wine opener. “I love the perfect angle on the foil cutter,” he says, “[and] I love that they tapped the knowledge of sommelier André Hueston Mack to make sure it worked well enough to be trusted by members of the industry. Seldom do I run into a product where I genuinely have a hard time choosing between different color variations like here, with the sleek matte black, pop of orange, or classy tortoise finish. But most of all, I love that this thing is guaranteed to work for life.”

MoMA Design Store Bodum Neon Nesting Mixing Bowls (Set of 4)

As a person who drinks coffee every day (and feels horrified when I run out), I would be thrilled to receive this American Girl doll-sized bag (weighing 4 pounds) of beans from the award-winning Joshua Tree Coffee. This year, the Big Bag — which is filled with the beans of your choice — even comes with a cute enamel mug.

Joshua Tree Coffee Big Bag & Bellied Enamel Mug Bundle

The Chitose is kind of like the Ferrari of kettles, because it boils water extremely fast and is made out of professional-grade, scratch-resistant 18-8 stainless steel. Plus, it cuts a cute silhouette and is compatible with induction top stoves.

Japanese Taste Chitose Induction Compatible Japanese Stainless Steel Kettle

These pastel eggnog petit fours come from the acclaimed Los Angeles-based confectionary Valerie Confections, and are made of a rich spiced buttercake, with bourbon ganache layers dipped in white chocolate and garnished with 23-karat gold leaf and chocolate biscuit pearls.

Ghia’s apéritif box is one of those drink-themed holiday gifts that sells out every year, because it pairs the brand’s signature amaro-esque N/A ambrosia with chic glassware from French-American glass artist and designer Sophie Lou Jacobsen. Whether you’re shopping for someone who doesn’t drink or is just trying to drink less alcohol in the new year, it’s a fashionable foot forward in the world of booze-free drinks.

Owning a double burner griddle is the culinary equivalent to flexing a California king size bed, because it can handle all of the pancakes, eggs, and grilled cheese orders from the family (without having to hop between skillets like a stove DJ). We love this one from Lodge, known for its excellent cast iron cookware.

Lodge Blacklock Triple Seasoned Cast Iron Double Burner Griddle

It’s likely that your giftee already owns cocktail glasses, but there’s also a non-zero chance that they’ve had a few stunners from their collection broken by jolly, wobbly party guests. Eater collaborated with heritage crystal glassware company Zwiesel Fortessa on a collection of timeless pieces, including this versatile set of six Nick and Nora-style glasses.

Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Folly Crystal Glass, 6 Ounce Cocktail (Set of 6)

Sometimes the best present is one that contains even more presents: a giant box of Swedish candies, all curated by the cult-fave confectioners at BonBon. Dubbed the Holiday Connoisseur Box, this light pink coffret is filled with classic BonBon gummies (I spy Pippi Longstocking’s Gold Coins) and plenty of Swedish classics like Marabou Japp chocolate bars and Juleskum marshmallow candies.

Kudos to Emma Chamberlain on this postmodern-feeling French press. The YouTuber went viral yet again for her collaboration with West Elm, and this coffee press in particularly takes notes from its elders (Bodum and Alessi) with its sleek stainless steel design.

Emma Chamberlain x West Elm Stainless Steel Button French Press

John Derian is the Final Boss of curating swish food-themed holiday ornaments (I do also need this energy drink-themed ornament), so it’s hardly surprising that the New York-based designer plucked this boneless cooked ham ornament for this year’s batch of stunners.

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

#6349. Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds

Robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.

Tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.

This isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.

Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.

But this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.

TeCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.

But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.

Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.

This unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.

But when they combine together, they unlock whole new operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.

Those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.

Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel

That being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. Currently, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do plan to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.

CSU / EurekAlert - Inspired by elephant trunks, these shape-shifting robots bend, grab and team up

M.H. Saikot et al - Tensegrity continuum robots enable task-adaptive morphologies for cooperative behaviours

UT - NASA Tests a Robotic Snake That Could Explore Other Worlds

UT - Snake Rovers Might be the Best Way to Explore the Surface and Tunnels on Mars

#6347. Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.

One of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.

Despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.

The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.

Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.

Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.

New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.

This image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille)

When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.

That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.

"We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.

This is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.

The researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.

"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions."

The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.

The researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.

Astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.

"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.

This is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.

"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.

More observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide important observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.

"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

#6346. What’s the Best Snow and Ice Melt? Here’s Why Using Rock Salt Shouldn’t Be Your Default Option.

When you need to keep the driveway ice-free, there’s a wide variety of ice melts to consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If the winter weather in recent years hasn’t already been causing some chaos, this year’s Super El Niño isn’t helping. Preparation is key. Setting down a layer of snow and ice melt (i.e., deicers) on your driveway and walkways before a snowstorm hits can save you a lot of time shoveling or snow blowing. But when you walk into the home improvement store, there might be more options than you were prepared for. Don’t worry, with just a little bit of information under your belt, you can choose the best ice melt for the job.

Not all ice melt is created equal. Some melts don’t work as well as others in subzero temperatures and won’t be effective against bonded ice. And some ice melt negatively affects nearby lawns and plants, or causes irritation and health issues for pets. Knowing the difference between the ingredients that power your snow and ice melts is important when choosing the right one for you.

Deicers work by exhibiting one of two thermal reactions: exothermic or endothermic. Exothermic materials, such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride, release heat when they come into contact with ice or snow. Endothermic materials, such as rock salt and calcium magnesium acetate, absorb heat from their surroundings (such as the sun) and use that heat to melt ice.

Because of this difference, exothermic ice melts perform better in subzero temperatures, and endothermic melts become less effective below 20 degrees Fahrenheit or so, especially at night. However, though exothermic reactions are stronger, they can also be more corrosive and less friendly to plants and animals. Blended melts may offer a good balance, which can help the melt work better in lower temperatures, but also be less corrosive and harmful to pets and plants.

Sometimes referred to as a deicer and often simply called “salt,” ice and snow melts can be made of different chemical compounds or blended to take advantage of their different attributes. This can make some less damaging to pavements or nearby plants. We put together a list of the most typical compounds that you’ll see sold by themselves or in a list of ingredients in blended options, which are the most common types you’ll see at stores.

These are some of the most common types of compounds used for melting ice and snow. Some are sold in their pure form or may be an ingredient in a blended formula.

Exothermic ice melt compounds, such as calcium chloride and magnesium chloride, work better in subzero temperatures because they release heat. If you live in an area where winter temperatures regularly drop below zero, consider one of these types or a blend that contains them.

If your winters are milder and average temperatures tend to hover in the twenties, an endothermic ice melt like rock salt or a urea blend can get the job done. Blended ice melts will often combine exothermic and endothermic compounds to help them perform better in lower temperatures and keep the cost more reasonable. Companies that make these blends will often label the bag with the lowest effective temperature to help you know for sure.

Traditional salts can irritate dog and cat paws, and some of the stronger exothermic compounds that include chlorides can also be irritating or harmful if ingested. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) says ingestion can lead to ice melt toxicosis, which can cause vomiting or neurological issues. However, ice melt toxicosis is unlikely to happen from just a few licks; the most serious cause is when a bag of melt is left unattended and ingested by your pet in large amounts.

To help combat this, many brands offer “pet safe” varieties of ice melt, but no blend is truly perfect. These animal-friendly blends tend to eliminate sodium or chloride from the mix, but not all do. The ASPCA recommends using urea-based ice melts, as urea (a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen) is the least likely ingredient to cause stomach irritation. Another simple idea, especially in cities and suburbs where there is little control over what ice melt the neighbors use, is to adorn your dog in paw booties before taking a walk.

Ice melts that have high concentrations of salts or chlorides can be problematic for vegetation and the environment in general. According to a study by Penn State Extension, when used in large amounts, simple rock salt (sodium chloride) can injure or kill plants near the treated pavement as it washes away, and further pollute waterways, harming fish and other marine life. Instead, the study notes, a compound like calcium magnesium acetate (CMA), which forgoes the use of chlorides or salts, is a safer option for environmentally sensitive areas. Urea-based ice melts are also a good choice.

Like the pet-friendly varieties of deicers, brands can be very loose with how they market their eco-friendly products, especially with the blends; there’s no guarantee that the one you buy won’t partially contain a compound that is harmful in large quantities. If you want to be as eco-friendly as possible, avoid blends that include chlorides and salts.

If that can’t be avoided, just follow the golden rule of “everything in moderation.” After all, overtreating an area is more likely to damage nearby vegetation—even if you use the more environmentally friendly varieties. If you’re still finding noticeable piles of deicer after the snow and ice are gone, you might be using too much.

Corrosion is a considerable problem caused by deicers. Salt-based melts or brines can penetrate porous stone, freeze, and cause the surface to expand. Meanwhile, chlorides can accelerate the rate of corrosion in metal. The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency noted that acetate-based deicers that don’t use chlorides or salts caused low to moderate levels of corrosion, but again, using any ice melt in moderation will help lower the chance of corrosion to your sidewalks, driveways, and nearby railings.

#6345. Highly Specific Observations While Scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards

The great dishes, gorgeous restaurants, and quirky cocktails that commanded our attention, even if they didn’t make the big list

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The past year has been one of “Great Chickenings” and fine dining flips, British food invasions and restaurants whose dining rooms feel like living rooms, vibrant global steakhouses and unserious Y2K food. Among the slate of our 2026 Eater Award winners — which also brought undeniable new chef talent, core-memory-forming dishes, and groundbreaking bakeries and bars — are the places we could not stop thinking about for highly specific reasons. While this crop of restaurants and bars did not make the ultimate cut for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, they commanded enough attention during our expansive scouting and research months to deserve acknowledgment. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Cabbage is having its moment. From a star turn on the Sandy Liang runway as a ruffled bag to a hand-painted Bordallo Pinheiro dinner set and a declaration from Vogue that the leafy green has gone “chic,” the cruciferous vegetable is 2026’s “it” girl. The cult of the cabbage has made its way to Monte’s in Montecito, a cozy Korean American bistro where cone cabbage gets coal-roasted and kissed with salty smoked shiitake XO, an umami-heavy spin on the Hong Kong-born sauce. The fall-apart-tender cabbage beds on creamy tofu puree, the whole thing studded with hazelnuts that bring out the vegetable’s innate sweetness. Preparations like the one at Monte’s make it feel as though cabbage isn’t just this year’s distinguished vegetable — its dominance is here to stay. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

Maybe it was the Negroni, the Old Fashioned, and the gingery mezcal-laced Missed Opportunity. Perhaps it was the jetlag (who can say for sure?), but the bathroom at Bobo — the Filipino bar attached to Muhajir in Chicago’s Lincoln Park — left a lasting impression on me. In a world that’s fully embraced the bathroom selfie, Bobo has answered the call with refractory horizontal-mirrored panel walls and colored light that shifts from reds to greens, turning this lavatory into a mesmerizing disco ball. It’s a fitting touch that matches chef Jacob Dela Cruz’s vision for a red-light district-esque tropical hideaway. — Brenna Houck, Eater editorial manager

In a world of outrageous martinis, the one at Greenpoint Malaysian restaurant Kelang earns its playful name. The Dirty Fish riffs on a Vesper with gin, vodka, dry vermouth, and, saliently, fish sauce, which levels up the drink’s savoriness in every way. The pungent condiment mimics olive brine, delivering a salty taste of the sea to the already strong drink, which then gets garnished with wavy scallions and a long sliver of aromatic ginger. The cocktail showcases owner Chris Low’s background as a Malaysian kid who grew up in New York. It’s simply presented — a cloudy drink in a stemmed coupe glass with those gloating garnishes — and pairs best with that fluffy paratha served over creamy and spicy dal. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

Gone may be the days of business power lunches at Wolfgang Puck’s Spago or Grill on the Alley that required a suit and tie. In their place, a new arrangement has emerged — the low-key power lunch. There may be no better place for the midday meal masquerading as a meeting right now than at Little Fish in Melrose Hill, the first full-service restaurant from the former pop-up-turned-fish sandwich window. The light-filled dining room hums during daytime with flexibly scheduled creatives and well-dressed parents toting young children, all adults in the room sipping wine picked by sommelier Kae Whalen. On the menu, a tuna melt from maverick chefs and owners Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle will convert even nonbelievers, especially when paired with peppery fries dunked in horseradish aioli. Of course, there is the calling card fried fish sandwich, but smarter diners go for the beach sandwich layered with guindilla peppers and soy-cured mussels and a bay leaf chip stracciatella flecked with chocolate chips. Melrose Hill and its confluence of independent restaurants has morphed into a miniature walkable neighborhood — the perfect place to see and be seen. And what’s more low-key power lunch than that? — RR

Historically, California is a gold mine of kitsch restaurants, from Clifton’s Republic to the pillowy pink dining room at the Madonna Inn. Night Hawk is the next jewel in that camp crown; the Greek-influenced San Diego restaurant is an anchor of Coronado Island’s hypermaximalist new Baby Grand hotel and beckons diners into a lush, faux-rock-filled outdoor dining room with pink clamshell chairs, waterfalls, and cocktails that have names like the Adonis in Bloom and Spanakopita Punch. In short: Tony Duquette by way of an acid tab. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

British food hit a fever pitch nationally this year as Americans awakened to the allure of meat pies and mushy peas. But if any restaurant truly dispelled notions of the country’s cuisine as dull or bland, it was Ambassadors Clubhouse, with its extensive menu of Punjabi showstoppers such as seven-layer, aloo-filed, Amritsari-style samosas; butter chicken in the form of lollipop-like chops with a heady char; and matka Beliram lamb, its crimson oil heralding intense flavor. In opulent, velvet-adorned surroundings that feel like a hideaway from the city, this luxe London import deliciously makes the case that Indian food is as essential to British cuisine as fish and chips. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

The most beautiful new restaurant in California is tucked into a shopping center in Montecito’s tony upper village. Little Mountain, which opened in November 2025 under chef Diego Moya, gives more to the scene than just a locavore menu that leans into live-fire cooking — it brings a bona fide, Architectural Digest-worthy destination that I would get married (and remarried) in. It may be hard to decide which room to sit in should you land a reservation in time: the comfortable dining room with gold-veil natural lighting and plush caramel booths and banquettes; the larger-party table that foregrounds an open kitchen and its centerpiece hearth; the dim, dark bar that may be the sexiest sliver of drinking den on the Central Coast; the covered patio that leads into a monarchial private dining area; or the outdoor patio that evokes dining in a home garden. Anywhere you sit, you can’t go wrong, especially as the food starts landing in front of you. — NF

Chef Theo Adley opened Heretík last spring, and it has brought a breath of fresh, San Sebastián-esque sea breeze air into the Denver dining scene. The French- and Basque-leaning restaurant serves an endless summer menu of dishes like Santa Barbara uni, a playful pan con tomate martini, and scallops à la plancha with bearnaise and seaweed. The menu’s coastal Euro allure gets amplified by its interior design choices, which sprinkle in vintage furniture and tapered, wax drip-laden candles — but with a name like Heretík, you know that all of that romance is going to come with a healthy dose of cheek. — FK

Chickens, you can’t take credit for this one: The British-inspired pub Dean’s proved that bigger is not always better with its take on a Scotch egg, which employs quail eggs instead of the typical chicken ones. In larger Scotch eggs, what appears in each bite can be inconsistent. But the result of the shrunken-down approach here is a reliably favorable ratio of meat to egg, in which each bite at once encompasses crunchy breading, tender meat filling, runny yolk, and just enough still-bouncy egg white. It’s as nonnegotiable at Dean’s as a pint of Guinness. — BM

Ladyfish in Portland, Maine, has been clear about one thing since the beginning: “A summer fling,” the restaurant declared when it announced its May 2026 arrival. Jordan and Marisa Rubin of Portland sushi spot Mr. Tuna convinced chef Christine Lau to relocate from New York City to helm the seasonal seafood pop-up. Lau, whose resume includes Japanese-Italian and Chino Latino restaurants, brings her distinctive flair to classic Maine ingredients for dishes like scallops in a blanket with fried milk bread and the showstopping twin lobster mountain served with fries, rice cakes, and dan dan au poivre sauce. True to its word, the restaurant closed at the end of October. Here’s hoping the return of next year’s summertime crowds also brings back this match made in seafood heaven. — Stephanie Wu, editor in chief

Los Angeles-born chef Ray Garcia opened Broken Spanish Comedor in Culver City in late 2025, years after his groundbreaking Mexican fine dining restaurant, Broken Spanish, and more casual B.S. Taqueria closed in Downtown Los Angeles. Garcia’s contribution to Alta California cuisine, rooted in Mexican cooking told through a California lens, remains one of the most distinct of this generation of restaurants. Still, he manages to surprise both longtime fans and newcomers to his work: The Comedor, whose name nods to the Indigenous homestyle restaurant tradition in Mexico, feels fresh in its A-frame home. It’s not uncommon for locals and those working in Los Angeles hospitality to stop in for a meal of crispy, crown-whorled chicharron or quesillo-threaded refried lentils; a classics-leaning drinks menu (cócteles, cervezas, vino) keeps the room humming happily. In a year brimming with big restaurant comebacks (see also: Venice’s resurrected Tasting Kitchen and Keith Corbin’s reframed Alta Adams), it feels good to have an Angeleno chef like Ray Garcia capture our collective imagination again. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

If ever there was a destination in need of effective hangover cures, it’s New Orleans. While I was totally ready to rally after a two-bar, two-restaurant evening the night before (I am, of course, a professional), I also wasn’t mad about consuming something fortifying at Casimiro, the charming all-day cafe from award-winning Acamaya chef Ana Castro, the next morning. The restaurant delivered: textbook chilaquiles, impossibly fluffy conchas, crispy pescaditos, and one of the best tortas I’ve ever had. If hair of the dog is in your future in the City That Always Drinks, go with the well-balanced Cynar daiquiri to finish. — Missy Frederick, dining editorial director

The weirdest thing I ate on a pastry this year was “lettuce cream” lacquered onto the BLT Danish at Dahlia in Minneapolis. The chartreuse-colored cream anchored a slice of late-August tomato and dollops of bacon jam atop persistently crisp laminated dough. One bite was enough to make me think, This should be more of a thing. You wouldn’t know at first glance that this bakery, tucked into an office complex, turns out treats of this caliber: jam-filled croissants with speculoos crumble, unassumingly perfect English muffins, plush milk bread and fluffy focaccia for sandwiches. This kind of out-of-the-box baking makes eating pastries right now so fun. — BM

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6343. LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date

An international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.

For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.

This new view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.

The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON

"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.

In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This new view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.

The other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.

The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON

According to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.

The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

#6342. A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

A geographer calls it Aquaterra. For 120,000 years, early humans lived there—then the oceans swallowed it.

Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke. Trying to leave no stone unturned, I explored the former colony’s dedicated National Historic Site, poured over archives of antique maps, and even took in a lavish outdoor stage production.

Ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks. Yet one moment from that trip has never been far from my mind, and it reshaped how I thought about our quest for answers about early human history.

It came about during a conversation with Dr. Eric Klingelhofer, a respected scholar and Vice President for Research with The First Colony Foundation. Dr. Klingelhofer had overseen several excavations that yielded remnants of Roanoke, but he was worried that many once-buried artifacts had already been claimed by a much more powerful force.

“Before my retirement,” he told me, “I attended a UNESCO-backed conference on Bonaire in the Dutch West Indies. These causes, rising sea levels and storm surges, plus coastal overdevelopment, endangered every island, as most prehistoric and early colonial sites lie close to the sea.” As we sat there on tranquil, federally protected land, it was hard for me to feel the urgency at the time, but he stressed that we were in a race against time. “At Fort Raleigh,”—the name the National Parks Service gave the National Historic Site—“coastal erosion has already swallowed up excavation units we had dug in 2007. The rate of loss is about twenty feet in twenty years—and it may be increasing.”

After our conversation, I walked along the island’s shoreline, struck by the thought that although I might be walking the same land as those colonists, the landscape wasn’t really the same. Their shoreline likely sat yards farther out than the one I strolled, and as the water swept that land away, it took with it our chance to learn more about the people who once stood there.

In the study of history, we too often focus on the preservation or replication of what was once on a certain parcel of land, taking it as a given that the land itself stayed constant. We spend all our time debating whether the proverbial Ship of Theseus is still the same after centuries of repairs, never stopping to question if the shoreline of Delos on which he landed still remains.

Yet, recent studies have emerged to remind us that even in the absence of human intervention, the world looked different to the peoples of the past than it does to us today.

The scale of this dilemma, the problem of our submerged history, is far greater than a single island in North Carolina, or a single colony from the 1500s. Our whole understanding of early humankind may be built on faulty ground, due specifically to how much of that ground is now underwater. But don’t let your thoughts drift to that Platonic idea of Atlantis; the proper term, as The Atlantic recently reminded us, is Aquaterra.

In 2014, the geographer Jerome E. Dobson mounted a case for the recognition of a global landmass he dubbed Aquaterra, a term he first proposed in 1999. In “Aquaterra Incognita,” Dobson argued that “all landmasses are defined by time as well as space,” and therefore, since “so little is known about the seacoast where a significant portion of humankind surely dwelled for the better part of 120,000 years,” we should properly recognize and name the 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass that once hosted the earliest human civilizations.

When we think about the ice ages that have cycled across Earth’s history, we can easily picture the glaciers and ice sheets that formed, but we rarely consider where all that water came from. During an ice age, sea levels drop, exposing land that’s now underwater. As a result, the shorelines early humans knew looked very different from the ones we see today.

The lowlands these glaciers exposed were not bereft of life, either. The ecosystems they once supported varied, from grasslands to wetlands, forests to estuaries. They attracted wildlife, and later, early human civilizations. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” Dobson writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.”

When the glaciers melted and sea levels rose again, naturally, early humans abandoned their soon-to-be-submerged settlements. But that doesn’t mean we should simply ignore what once stood there. “It would not change the timeline of human progress if, for instance, cities were found as low as -50 meters, since Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were that low,” Dobson notes. What could revise that timeline, he notes, is “the possibility that precursors of major innovations may exist at even lower depths.”

“One intriguing possibility is pottery,” he proposes:

All this talk about “possibility,” of course, makes the benefits of recognizing Aquaterra seem entirely theoretical. Yet in just the last few years, the archeological world received a stirring reminder that the land we can see is not the only land there ever was, and that whole chapters of our history may have been claimed by the sea.

In 2021, Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith published “The magnificent seven: Marine submerged precontact sites found by systematic geoarchaeology in the Americas.” The study documented not one or two but seven projects, in North America alone, that had found traces of precontact life now drowned beneath the continental shelf. Each of the seven projects worked “from the terrestrially known, to the submerged unknown.” Using methodical but varied mapping and modeling techniques, researchers predicted where people might once have lived, then searched for proof with underwater surveys, sediment cores, and even hands-on excavations.

One of the research efforts happened in the Gulf of Mexico’s paleo-Sabine River. Over the course of a decade, from 1976 to 1986, it turned up “charred wood and vegetation, nut hulls, seeds, fish scales, and bone from fish, reptiles, birds, and small mammals,” some of which dated back 9,000 years. Soon after, researchers in Belize found the drowned outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings, which turned out to be Classic-period Maya salt works now sitting underwater. Other research discussed in the study uncovered stone tools, campsites, and even a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.

To truly understand human history, we can’t keep digging only in the land we can see. We also have to search for the land our ancestors knew, much of which now lies beneath the waves. That calls for a change in mindset and a rethinking of how archaeology works. As seas keep rising, how many more once-inhabited places will slip beneath the surface, taking with them secrets as recent as Roanoke’s? If we don’t change course now, the sites we have yet to excavate may be written off by tomorrow’s scholars as mere seafloor.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

#6341. SpaceX Launches Starship But Passes Up Booster Catch for Safety's Sake

SpaceX sent its Starship on a flight that was meant to feature a first-ever retrieval of both rocket stages, but a launch-pad catch of the first-stage booster had to be canceled due to safety concerns.

Instead, the Super Heavy booster was diverted during its descent to make an offshore splashdown. Observers at SpaceX's Starbase on the South Texas coast could hear the sonic boom and see the fiery plunge that took place minutes after launch at 4:47 p.m. CT (2247 GMT) today. "Wow, you could feel the rumble of that splashdown there," launch commentator Jessie Anderson said.

This 15th flight test still has a chance to make history: The mission plan calls for the Starship second stage to spend as much as 22 hours in orbit â ending with a return to the pad for a midair capture by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms. SpaceX has caught Starship's booster during three previous test flights, but this would be a first for a second stage.

Hours after launch, SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice said the booster's control system triggered an abort of the launch-tower catch because the boostback engine burn ended early, apparently due to a low fuel mass alarm. SpaceX's team was still troubleshooting the root cause of the alarm, she said.

Anderson said the offshore splashdown averted the risk of damage or injuries at the launch site. "Safety is always our No. 1 priority," she said. If any further safety concerns arise, SpaceX's mission team has the option of ending the flight early and sending the second stage â known as Ship 42 â down to a controlled ocean splashdown.

After reaching orbit, Ship 42 deployed 26 satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. Three of the satellites were equipped with a suite of cameras to inspect Ship's heatshield after deployment.

Starship ranks as the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, standing 407 feet (124 meters) tall and providing 17 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. The rocket is designed to deploy dozens of Starlink V3 satellites at a time â and eventually send thousands of explorers and settlers to Mars.

NASA is counting on SpaceX to provide a Starship-based system for landing astronauts on the moon by as early as 2028. As a preparatory step, NASA is planning to test Starship as well as Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system in low Earth orbit next year. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman referred to that test mission, known as Artemis III, in a post to X that took note of the video sent down from orbit via the Starlink network.

"Congratulations to the SpaceX team on another spectacular launch," Isaacman wrote. "Very much appreciate how you bring the world along in high resolution. We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III."

This report has been updated with further details about the aborted booster catch.

#6340. Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.

California is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada. But scientists are discovering that the state’s insect diversity is far greater than previously believed.

A new study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates. Scientists have formally described only about two-thirds of them. Led by researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, the study also found that nearly every location sampled had its own distinct insect community.

The findings suggest that conserving California’s insect life will require protecting a wide range of habitats. Even places with similar climates and landscapes can harbor different species, making it difficult for any single protected area to represent the state’s extraordinary diversity.

The research is the first publication from the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project with an ambitious goal: collect and identify every insect species in California. Although insects are the most diverse group of animals on land, they remain underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments.

Researchers used DNA barcoding on more than one million insect specimens. The technique compares short sections of DNA to help distinguish species, giving scientists a way to investigate diversity that can be difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

The effort brought together the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, and California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Researchers gathered tissue samples from museum collections, deployed Malaise traps across 72 ecoregions, and made collecting expeditions to 454 additional locations statewide.

Museum specimens extended the project’s reach beyond what researchers could collect in the field. Fresh sampling added another essential piece, with volunteers helping keep traps operating week after week. Although Malaise traps capture insects passively, collecting their contents and maintaining them takes sustained effort.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” says study co-author Giar-Ann Kung, the museum’s entomology collections manager.

Kung joined researchers and volunteers across California in setting traps and collecting insects. Some participants maintained sampling sites for years, providing a continuity that the research team could not have achieved alone.

“There are people like Sara Fairchild and Michael Nance who managed a Malaise trap for over three years at a site in the high desert, which is the longest continuous site for the project. That could not have been accomplished without them.”

To explore how insect diversity varies across California, the researchers compared ecoregions, areas grouped by the Environmental Protection Agency according to shared ecosystem characteristics. They used Level 3 classifications, including the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. Of these regions, the Mojave Basin and Range had the greatest number of insect species.

Although similar environments shared some patterns, each region had its own mix of insects. “The deserts are kind of more similar to each other, and the mountains in northern California are a little bit more similar to each other, but every part of the state hosts a really different insect fauna,” says Dr. Barkdull.

Those differences also appeared at a smaller scale, with individual collecting sites within the same ecoregion harboring distinct insect communities. Together, the findings highlight the need to protect a wide range of California’s wild places.

Reference: “DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California’s insect biodiversity remains undiscovered” by Austin J.
