#6280. A massive buried church in Old Dongola is larger than the White House, but archaeologists have only dug down to a single staircase so far

At Old Dongola in Sudan, a church about 154 feet wide and 187 feet long is still mostly unexcavated, and a monumental staircase is now exposed.

Inside the medieval citadel of Old Dongola, in Sudan, a Sudanese-Polish team has cleared a monumental staircase that leads into a church still almost entirely unexcavated.

In that stairwell, the archaeologists reached the building’s original floor for the first time.

Artur Obłuski of the University of Warsaw now puts the Great Church of Jesus at 154 feet (47 meters) wide and about 187 feet (57 meters) long.

He says that makes it larger than the White House, although the team has examined only a small part of it and the final size is still open.

The expedition first came across the building in 2021. Old Dongola was then the focus of work funded by the European Research Council, and the team was cleaning the wall of an apse, the curved end of a church that holds the altar.

The university’s 2021 report gave the church a width of about 85 feet (26 meters) and the apse a diameter of about 20 feet (6 meters). That apse was already the largest found in Nubia. Murals on its walls showed two rows of monumental figures.

The new figure of 154 feet follows the latest season. Workers also exposed the buttresses that reinforce the apse. Obłuski cautiously estimates the height at 69 feet (21 meters).

The university describes the building as probably the largest church of medieval Nubia. Arabic sources call it the richest.

Good preservation has become the main obstacle. Part of the stairwell wall survives to about 36 feet (11 meters), so the trenches must go unusually deep and need far more resources than a normal dig.

Obłuski said the team wants to settle the size of the church next season. Speaking in the university’s Polish-language statement, he compared the building with the presidential residence in Washington and added a plan for it. The next two quotes are our translation from the Polish.

“This is a building larger than the famous White House in Washington,” he said. “And we plan to dig it out.”

Old Dongola was the capital of Makuria, a Christian kingdom on the Nile. The Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology has worked in the region since 1964, and a 17th-century paper from the site recently helped confirm a long-debated Nubian king.

Until now, specialists treated a different church, outside the citadel, as the cathedral of Dongola. Obłuski said in the new statement that scholars will probably have to reconsider what that building was for.

In the 2021 report, he said the find “will radically change the knowledge” of the city and of the Nubian church. The team compared the layout with Faras, where a cathedral stood at the center of the citadel with a bishop’s domed tomb to its east.

At Old Dongola, a domed building about 25 feet (7.5 meters) across adjoins the apse.

The cathedral identification remains a working conclusion. The 2021 report said the church may have housed an archbishop responsible for about 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) of the Nile, between the 1st and 5th cataracts (rapids).

In the same statement Obłuski compared the church to Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, calling such buildings “trendsetters” (our translation) for planning and engineering. He described the Great Church as a natural candidate for that role in Nubia, and perhaps in that part of Africa.

The dig also produced a surprise. A second, smaller church stood on the upper floor of a structure added to the Great Church, and its walls survive to only about 3 feet (1 meter).

Traces of painting remained on those walls. Fragments of painted plaster from the room now fill six large shelving units.

Obłuski contrasted this with a similar annex on the north side, connected to the Makurian King David in the 13th century, which the team found in 2023 with its paintings still on the walls.

In the debris of the smaller church, excavators recovered small pieces of plaster with Greek writing. Agata Deptuła, the expedition’s epigrapher, identified them as biblical canticles, or odes, which are prayer songs added to the book of Psalms.

One fragment comes from the prayer of Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel in the Old Testament. A scribe wrote it in a careful book hand, with letters only about a fifth of an inch (half a centimeter) tall.

Deptuła said Old Dongola had mostly yielded psalm texts until now, which makes the odes new for the site. At Hippos, above the Sea of Galilee, Greek inscriptions fixed the last known renovation of a Byzantine cathedral with two baptism rooms.

The Great Church is also separate from the Sudanese church built around a carving of a possible Kushite ruler at Miseeda.

Flooding in autumn 2024, the worst at Old Dongola since 1988, damaged some of the roofs that shelter the monuments.

Before digging resumed, the team stabilized the site together with the Faculty of Civil Engineering at Warsaw University of Technology.

The expedition also built a solar power installation, paid for by Poland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs through its Polish Aid program. It powers the motors of pumps that bring Nile water to the homes and fields of about 10,000 people.

Obłuski said the team added an installation for eight stations that raise water pressure, so homes on higher ground can be supplied. The conflict in Sudan had left those residents without water.

The work runs with Sudan’s National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums and with local residents, who formed an association to help care for the site. During the last season, the archaeologists also joined local evening meals that break the fast at Ramadan.

The 187-foot length is approximate, and the 69-foot height is an estimate. Only the stairwell has reached floor level, so the plan of the interior remains largely unknown.

The university’s statement is a news report and not a peer-reviewed paper. It gives no construction date for the church and does not name any odes beyond Hannah’s prayer.

For now, the original floor of the Great Church is known only at the bottom of one staircase.

The information was obtained from the University of Warsaw.

#6279. The 8 Best Outdoor Pizza Ovens That Deliver Delicious Homemade Pies

We tested the Ooni Karu 2, Ninja Artisan, Gozney Tread, and others to find out which models are worth the dough.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like tending to the grill and gathering around a firepit are inherently enjoyable, enjoying a fresh, piping-hot pizza is similarly rewarding, and it’s just a bit more special when it’s homemade. Baking a pie in the oven can yield good results, but there’s nothing like the crunchy crust and smoky flavor of a pizza made in a proper hearth. If you’re hoping to replicate your favorite restaurant’s pie, an outdoor pizza oven can take your homemade slices from decent to genuinely artisan.

Stand-alone and countertop outdoor pizza ovens reach much higher temperatures than regular ovens, and in less time. That high heat is exactly what you need for a perfectly cooked pizza crust—and several of the models we tested can cook up a pie in as little as 60 seconds.

Plus, many of the best outdoor pizza ovens we write about are suited for cooking other tasty foods, just like a real hearth. You can make fish, meat, roasted vegetables, and even bread in these wood-fired and gas-fueled models.

To find the best pizza ovens, we looked at models with good features and designs and called in a handful to try out for ourselves. We selected pizza ovens that use a variety of fuels, including gas, charcoal, and wood. Outdoor pizza ovens all pretty much come with a learning curve, but we identified models best suited to beginners and pizza aficionados alike to offer a range that caters to different skill levels.

For testing, we heated each oven for 30 minutes to season them and burn off any oils or contaminants from manufacturing, then let them cool completely. Fifteen minutes after firing up each oven on high using propane burners, we measured the temperatures on the pizza stones with an infrared thermometer.

Then, we made pizza, using the same dough each time, with propane and oak firewood as our fuel. During cooking, we noted how well each oven performed, different features, and its ease of use. Finally—and most enjoyably—we assessed (a.k.a. ate) the pizza. We recommend the following pizza ovens based on our hands-on experience, their specs, and quality.

Over a decade ago, Ooni built its first portable pizza oven with a design that many have mimicked. Our previous pick for the best pizza oven, the Karu 16, has been replaced by the Karu 2 Pro. It’s the exact same as the Karu 16 with three new features: an air vent, Bluetooth-connected thermometer, and an even larger window on the oven door.

Like the Karu 16, the Karu 2 Pro makes 16-inch pizzas fired either with propane or wood. In testing, we liked the locking door with a glass window, which helped maintain a consistent temperature and allowed us to keep an eye on our pizza while it cooked.

Ooni also added a digital thermometer to this model that monitors air temperature in the oven via a wired probe. That info is sent to your phone so you can be in the kitchen prepping more pies or enjoying company instead of babysitting the oven.

Using the propane burner is easy and gets the job done, but we appreciate the large firebox for wood, which provides a lot more flame across the top of the oven. The large capacity also had us refilling it less frequently than smaller wood-fired ovens.

The Karu 2 Pro also doubles as a capable charcoal grill if you want to cook meat or veggies. While we like a dedicated grill for burgers and steaks, the Karu 2 is a do-it-all outdoor kitchen if you have limited outdoor space. The addition of the new air vent even gets it down to a consistent 200 degrees Fahrenheit for low-and-slow cooking.

Full Ooni Karu 2 Multi-Fuel Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Ninja Artisan is the only electric outdoor pizza oven we've come across that's worth a double take. It needs to be covered if left outside because of the electrical components, but the body is made of weather-resistant steel.

Our tester, Danny Perez, didn’t have to hassle with pellets or propane to get things started—he simply plugged it in, preheated, and started cooking. It has a max temp of 700 degrees Fahrenheit, which is less than most gas and wood-fired ovens, but it's not necessarily a bad thing.

While a 1,000-degree oven that makes pizza in 90 seconds sounds easy, there's a lot more to it. Shredded mozzarella starts melting in seconds, the dough crust needs a minute to bake, and toppings may require a different cooking time. Electric temperature controls and a lower max heat offer more runway before taking off on your pizza-making journey. Another plus of an electric outdoor pizza oven is even cooking because there's no need to turn the pizza when it's in the oven.

The Ninja has built-in preset pizza modes to cook different styles of 'za: Neapolitan, New York, thin crust, and pan. It preheats to respective target temps for each and then prompts you to add the pizza. Hit start and it starts counting down for a perfectly timed cook.

He tried the thin crust setting, which cooked the pizza at 550 degrees Fahrenheit for four minutes. When the timer went off, out came an evenly cooked pepperoni pizza.

The Neapolitan setting worked great as well. It cooked the pizza at 700 degrees F for two and a half minutes yielding an impressively crisped crust with some leopard spotting.

Full Ninja Artisan Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

A lot of outdoor pizza ovens are portable enough to pick up and move, but they aren't designed with transportation in mind. Fair—most of us park them in the backyard. Gozney put more thought into portability than its competitors with the Tread pizza oven.

It weighs 30 pounds, has two handles on top, and has a manageable square shape. It can go from home to tailgate with ease. We tested the Tread with the collapsible Venture Stand, which gives you a cooking space wherever you take it.

Getting the Tread fired up only takes a few seconds when using the control dial on the side. The flames instantly extended across the roof of the pizza oven, and we wanted things to get hot, so we preheated for about 20 minutes. Once it reached an optimal temperature, we were ready to pitch the first pizza.

The compact size can fit up to 12-inch pies, which is plenty big for personal pizzas. In testing, we found that the oven has great heat retention, so you can cook them one after another. We also found the opening offered enough wiggle room to rotate the pie with a pizza peel for even cooking.

The Tread comes with a built-in thermometer on the side, but we still used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature of the pizza stone itself. The quick-release gas hose and regulator make for quick setup, too. For those who plan to take the Tread on the go, Gozney also has a handy carrying case.

Full Gozney Tread Portable Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

You'd be hard-pressed to find an electric pizza oven that gets the job done like the original Ooni Volt, but the Ooni Volt 2 is an honorable step up. This model has a smaller carbon footprint than its predecessor, and it's even easier to use.

Messing with temperatures can get complicated quickly, but the Volt 2 has three presets for cooking Neapolitan, New York, and Chicago Deep Dish-style pizzas to perfection. We usually use an infrared thermometer to gauge the temperature of pizza stones, but we trusted the presets and weren't disappointed.

While this electric pizza oven doesn't exactly mimic a wood-fired or propane-fueled model, it has its place in the kitchen. The Volt 2 can be used all year long, is capable of cooking plenty of your favorites, and is much easier to manage. Even if you already have an outdoor model, we'd go so far as to say that you might need this indoor version, too.

Full Ooni Volt 2 Electric Pizza Oven Review

Typically, rotating pizza stones are a gimmick you find on budget pizza ovens to make up for a low temperature range, especially for an electric model. GreenPan’s Stanley Tucci pizza oven, however, has both firepower and a surprisingly effective rotating stone for indoor and outdoor use.

The controls on this model go from 350 to 850 degrees Fahrenheit, so you can use it for more than just cooking pizza. The oven also has a temperature boost feature that allows you to “boost” the top, bottom, or both heating elements. During testing, Ford used this to crisp up the top crust and brown the edges, and this feature offered more flexibility for cooking his pizza exactly how he liked it.

The Stanley Tucci pizza oven uses a round stone, which sometimes can make it harder to accurately pitch your creation onto the stone. With this model, the oven door has a mechanism attached so that when you open it, the stone is lifted and pulled out, making it easier to toss in your pizza and avoid accidental spills and messes.

Overall, this is the best electric rotating pizza oven that Ford has tried yet, though he noted that this design is limited to 12-inch pizzas only.

Full GreenPan Stanley Tucci Pizza Oven Review

The Gozney Dome Gen2 is definitely a luxury pizza oven, but it's chock-full of features that could potentially make it a worthy investment for those who are dedicated to perfecting their pizza and baking crafts.

A 14-inch flue sits atop the roof of the oven, and this was helpful for maintaining airflow and flames. The Dome Gen2 comes with a standard propane burner, and the wood kit is optional. This helps simplify the process for newer pizza-makers, since wood-fired cooking takes some time to master.

One of the highlights we appreciate the most is the size of the oven itself. After preheating, we had no problem cooking two midsize pizzas side-by-side, and we could move the pies around if we needed to slow the cook time.

It takes a little longer for the oven to heat up when using wood, but luckily, changing the fuel mode doesn't make the burner obsolete. We were able to fire up the oven with the burner first, then switched to wood when it reached the right temperature and turned off the propane.

We tested the Dome Gen2 on a somewhat windy day, and the propane burner blew out a few times. To offset this, we kept the temperature a little higher than usual and burned charcoal on the wood tray for better control.

The digital display is a very convenient feature. Instead of using an infrared thermometer, we could monitor levels in real time right on the pizza oven without worrying about accuracy.

Full Gozney Dome Gen2 Dual Fuel Pizza Oven Review

A pizza oven from the smokeless firepit folks? Sign us up. The ease of cooking with a propane burner is tough to beat.

It took us about 20 minutes to heat up the oven using propane, though you should expect a bit more time when it’s relatively cool out and less when it’s hot. In testing, the average cook time was about 90 seconds and required turning the pie every 20 seconds or so.

The Pi Prime’s manual not only had thorough assembly instructions but a lot of helpful notes and tips to get started, including suggested target temperatures for different styles of pizza.

We found that managing oven and stone temperatures didn’t take too much time, although like other ovens without a door, breezy or windy days could make it more challenging. The oven opening on the Pi is 13 inches wide, so 12-inch pies are about as big as this oven can handle.

Similar to Solo Stove fire pits, ventilation holes line the bottom of the pizza oven for plenty of airflow. The Pi Prime is also constructed with durable 304 stainless steel to withstand high temps and different weather conditions.

Full Solo Stove Pi Prime Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Arc Lite is about as analog as it gets, equipped with only a pizza stone, ignition knob, and stainless steel insulated housing to bake your favorite pies. While this model is smaller and less features-heavy than the Dome Gen2 we’ve tested, that doesn’t mean it’s any less effective.

It didn’t take long for us to get the Arc Lite up and running. We just connected the hose to the propane tank then pressed and turned the knob to ignite. It took about 20 minutes for the pizza oven to warm up on a cooler spring day, and we maintained an internal temperature of 800 degrees Fahrenheit. The Arc Lite reaches 950, but that high heat requires more attention so you don’t overcook your pie.

The pizza we made was ready in about 90 seconds and had the crunchy crust and bubbly cheese we desired, and the only downside we really came across during testing is that the Arc Lite is limited on size and can only cook up to 12-inch pizzas. Great for everyday bites, but not ideal if you’re looking to host and make multiple pies at once.

Full Gozney Arc Lite Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

Our resident pizza oven expert, Brad Ford, is regularly trying new models to consider for this roundup. In cases where we remove a model we’ve tested in favor of something new, we still like to highlight it here.

The All-Clad Rotating Stone Outdoor Pizza Oven was our previous pick for the best rotating design. It runs on four AA batteries and only requires a push button to start. But for this particular feature, Ford prefers the GreenPan Stanley Tucci Indoor and Outdoor Pizza Oven. It had clear benefits during his testing experience, and the unique lifting mechanism under the round stone made it easier to pitch pizzas into the oven.

Outdoor pizza ovens use gas or wood to create flames across the top that radiate intense heat downward, warming the pizza stone—like preheating an oven in your house. However, unlike your home oven, outdoor pizza ovens can reach up to 950 degrees Fahrenheit.

Once the outdoor pizza oven hits cooking temperature and your pizza is placed inside, it only takes a couple of minutes to cook. The pizza stone or oven floor gets to the same temperature as the roof so the pizza cooks fast and evenly. While it cooks, those flames up top produce a golden crust that’s crispy on the outside and soft and airy on the inside. Because the pizza only takes a minute or so to cook, you can make a few with different toppings one after another.

Wood is the traditional fuel of choice for pizza ovens, favored for the smoky flavor it imparts in the crust and toppings. However, wood (or charcoal) fires take longer to heat up and require more attention to maintain the right temperature. That may not be an issue if you’re only making a couple of pies, but it can become a hassle if you’re cooking multiple pies for a large group, or entertaining a party while you cook.

Propane fuel can heat a pizza oven up rather quickly. Since it only takes around 15 to 20 minutes to preheat, it's hard to deny the convenience of being able to cook a pie in a relatively short time frame. Plus, cleanup is easy when there’s no ashy firebox to empty. Just keep in mind that a propane oven won't give you that unique, wood-fired flavor.

Luckily, you don't have to sacrifice one for the other: A few of the brands we recommend offer extra accessories you can buy to accommodate a different fuel type. There are even some options with combined fuel, so you can heat up your oven fast with the propane and imbue the pizza with wood-fired flavor, too.

The oven’s size determines the maximum temperature output the unit can reach, as well as the size of pie you can cook. Most outdoor pizza ovens are designed for 12- or 14-inch pies. Our Best Overall pick, though, can accommodate pizzas up to 16 inches for oversized, restaurant-like slices.

Pizzas are typically cooked between 450 and 600 degrees Fahrenheit. Classic Neapolitan pizza requires temperatures around 900 degrees—these are the ones with golden crusts, mottled with dark leopard spots. High-end models top out at around 950 degrees Fahrenheit.

The pizza ovens we recommend have max temperatures that far exceed 500 degrees, but note that an oven with a relatively low maximum temperature still gives you a delicious, cooked-through pie—it just may not look quite as picture-perfect.

In short, yes. Outdoor pizza ovens are incredibly versatile. Beyond pies, you can cook meats like steak and chicken, roast veggies, bake bread (like sourdough or focaccia), prep seafood, make cast-iron dishes, and bake desserts. Since it's essentially a super-hot wood-fired oven, you can use plenty of different methods to whip up your favorite foods.

Accessories aren't necessarily a requirement for operating your pizza oven, but they can make the process a lot smoother and safer. We recommend using tools such as a pizza peel to move and adjust your pie, an infrared thermometer to check stone temp accurately, heat-resistant gloves, and a brush or scraper for cleaning the stone.

Outdoor pizza ovens are generally easy to clean and don't require a ton of maintenance since their high temperatures naturally burn off a majority of food residue. Usually, you can just brush off ash and debris after the oven has cooled down. You can also occasionally run it at high heat to get rid of any extra stubborn bits, and wipe down the exterior as needed. Avoid using water or soap on the pizza stone to prevent cracking.

#6278. Archaeologists Uncover 3,800-Year-Old Burial Mystery on Spain’s Coast

A burial ground on Spain’s southern coast suggests ancient communities may have continued building massive shared tombs during the Bronze Age, rather than simply reusing older monuments.

A 3,800-year-old burial mystery on Spain’s southern coast is challenging what archaeologists thought they knew about prehistoric burial traditions.

At a time when communities across the Iberian Peninsula were abandoning massive communal tombs in favor of smaller, individual graves, people near the Strait of Gibraltar appear to have continued burying their dead together. Even more puzzling, the stone monuments they used may have been newly constructed rather than inherited from earlier generations.

The discovery comes from the Trafalgar necropolis, where archaeologists investigated two collective tombs containing the remains of multiple individuals.

Radiocarbon dating of 16 individuals places the use of these tombs between 1875 and 1625 BC, making them among the latest known examples of collective megalithic burial in Iberia.

But the age of the human remains is only part of the mystery. Archaeologists also found no evidence of earlier occupation at the site, raising the possibility that the monuments themselves were constructed during the Bronze Age, when such building traditions were thought to be fading.

The study, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz in Spain and colleagues.

Determining when a tomb was used is not the same as establishing when it was built. Elsewhere in Iberia, Bronze Age communities sometimes buried their dead inside monuments dating back to the Copper Age, making it difficult to distinguish new construction from the reuse of older structures.

Trafalgar may represent an important exception. The absence of evidence for an earlier burial ground suggests the cemetery could have been established in the early second millennium BC. However, additional dating methods are needed to determine when the monuments were originally constructed.

The authors explain, “The Trafalgar megalithic necropolis has revealed a highly significant finding. During the Bronze Age, an entirely new funerary space was constructed in a landscape dominated by the sea. We propose this hypothesis based on the absence of archaeological evidence for earlier occupation in the surrounding area. Until now, the evidence available for this period has primarily pointed to the reuse of megalithic monuments built during the Copper Age. This discovery offers a new perspective on funerary practices during this period and would demonstrate that new monumental burial spaces continued to be constructed.”

The excavations also uncovered grave goods, including gold and copper earrings, silver beads, and an ivory comb, offering additional clues about the people buried at the site.

If further research confirms that the monuments were newly built during the Bronze Age, Trafalgar would provide rare evidence that monumental communal burial traditions survived longer than previously recognized.

Researchers believe additional tombs may remain undiscovered, potentially offering further insight into ancient Iberian burial traditions. However, strong coastal winds and shifting sands threaten to bury the site beneath the dunes again, making continued preservation essential for future excavations.

Reference: “The last builders of megaliths in the South of the Iberian peninsula? The Bronze Age necropolis of Trafalgar (Barbate, Cádiz, Spain)” by Eduardo Vijande-Vila, Serafín Becerra-Martín, Berta Morell-Rovira, Marta Díaz-Zorita Bonilla, Eduardo Molina-Piernas, Alejandro Muñoz-Muñoz, Adolfo Moreno-Márquez, Pablo González-Fernández, Salvador Domínguez-Bella, María Leticia Gómez-Sánchez, Diego Salvador Fernández-Sánchez, José Luis Ramírez-Amador, José María Corona-Borrego, María Carmona-Gil, Jesús Corrales Díaz and Juan Jesús Cantillo-Duarte, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. #6277. Rock shelter full of old charcoal suggests that Neanderthals burned 24 pounds of wood per day and had a cleaning system

Researchers mapped 640 charcoal fragments from a Neanderthal camp and found two distinct zones of burned wood.

From 2019 to 2022, excavators at Abric Romaní in Capellades, Spain, picked 640 charcoal fragments out of one layer of sediment by hand. They logged the position of every piece.

The largest measured about half an inch (13 millimeters). Together the pieces show where Neanderthals burned wood about 60,000 years ago, and where some of the waste may have gone.

Most of the charcoal lay around hearths near the shelter wall. Smaller patches lay to the south, and the study’s authors say those could be cleared hearth waste, though charcoal alone cannot prove it.

The layer is known as Level Ra. IPHES-CERCA, the Catalan institute that works at the site, calls it a Neanderthal camp specialized in deer hunting.

Amador Romaní discovered the shelter in 1909. The current project began in 1983, and more than 200 hearths have been identified. A wooden club with no clear parallel also came from this site.

Sediment built up fast here, at up to 31 inches (80 centimeters) per thousand years in Level Ra. The team did not sieve it, because sieving could have broken the charcoal. The authors note that hand-picking can bias the sample.

Crews took three-dimensional coordinates for each fragment by hand and with a total station, a surveying instrument. The 2022 season aimed to finish the whole surface of Level Ra.

On Aug. 19 of that year, the crew working in Level Rb lifted bone pieces coated in mineral crust. Specialists identified them as part of a Neanderthal skull.

Irene Cazalla, a restoration technician at IPHES-CERCA, then conserved them. The institute said no Neanderthal remains had turned up in more than 40 years of research at the site.

Tomás Fernández-Iriarte of IPHES-CERCA analyzed the charcoal and wrote the first draft, the paper’s author statement says. The work ran on an Olympus BX41 microscope at up to 500 times magnification.

The team checked its identifications against a collection of modern charred wood kept at the institute. A total of 484 fragments, about 76 percent, came from the Pinus sylvestris type. That group covers three mountain pines with very similar wood.

Those pines live today above about 1,970 feet (600 meters). The authors think their range was probably wider during the Ice Age.

Compression wood showed up in 501 fragments. It is a growth trait tied to stress and is common in branches. The authors say the occupants most likely burned branches, but more tree-ring work is needed to separate them from trunks.

A test on 100 fragments gave an alteration score of 0.55, within the range for rotten wood. The authors read this as a sign that the fuel was deadwood in varying states, moderately rotten, though the test covered only that subsample and not every wood type separately.

The paper cites ethnographic reports on small groups of five or six people in temperate climates. Those groups used up to 24 pounds (11 kilograms) of wood per day.

With that much to haul, the authors think the wood did not travel far. Mountain pines drop a lot of dead wood, so the people in the shelter probably took what lay nearby.

Squares R60 and S59 of the excavation grid held something different. The team found a group of Prunus charcoal there, from a genus represented by only 17 fragments in the whole sample.

The authors listed kindling or the extraction of a specific resource as possible reasons. They also raised fruit gathering, but no fruit or seeds have turned up in this level.

The northern sector held 495 fragments and the southern sector 145. The team mapped them with Kernel Density Estimation, a method that turns scattered points into a density surface.

Squares U53, T57, T54 and U56 were the densest, at 68 to 87 fragments per grid unit. They sit inside a larger spread from U51 to U59, beside the wall and on top of the hearths.

Southern patches reached 51 to 68 fragments per grid unit and overlapped less with hearths. The authors wrote that this pattern “could be explained by discrete hearth-cleaning events.”

Excavators have proposed a dump with burned bones in Level M and drop-and-toss areas in Level O. At Hohle Fels Cave in Germany, analyses found dumped residues from hearths, including some tied to Neanderthal occupations.

Other research has compared Neanderthal and Homo sapiens living spaces and explored early Neanderthal ideas of home.

Water flowed out of the rock walls here and carried minerals over the floor. Mineral inclusions marked 47.6 percent of the fragments.

The team first logged small reddish dots on the charcoal as “spores.” An electron microscope at Rovira i Virgili University showed they were iron deposits that formed later.

Fungal threads called hyphae appeared in 15.7 percent of the pieces. The southern sector had proportionally more of them, along with more mineral alteration.

The authors call the southern patches compatible with displacement or maintenance of hearths, but say their position alone “is insufficient to demonstrate such processes.” Weathering and water could also have shaped them.

Charcoal also cannot show if the fires belonged to one stay or several. One group may have cleared its own hearths. A later group may have come back after a gap and reused old fire spots.

Bones, stone tools and a geoarchaeological study of the hearths still have to be mapped across the same floor. The authors say they are working to upload the data, which is available on request for now.

Level Ra is fully excavated, and its 640 pieces of burned wood now exist as points on a grid.

The full study was published in the Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6275. A Strange Liquid Is Helping Scientists Overcome a Major Barrier in Nanotechnology

By filling the tiny pores of fragile materials with an unusual liquid, scientists have found a way to create intricate patterns without destroying their structures.

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) contain networks of tiny pores that can trap gases, capture pollutants, and support chemical reactions. These properties make them attractive for advanced sensors and electronic devices, but their fragile structures are easily damaged by the processes used to manufacture such devices. Researchers in Japan have now developed a way to carve precise patterns into these materials at room temperature without causing the extensive structural damage normally associated with the process.

The technique, developed at Tokyo University of Science (TUS), involves filling the pores of MOFs with an ionic liquid before exposing them to a focused ion beam. In experiments, the liquid strengthened a copper-based MOF and substantially reduced damage, allowing researchers to produce intricate features only a few hundred nanometers wide.

The origins of MOFs trace back to 1974, when University of Melbourne chemistry professor Richard Robson began exploring whether molecules and chemical bonds could replace the wooden balls and metal rods used in structural models. His experiments with copper ions connected by four-armed organic molecules helped establish the foundations of a new class of porous materials. Today, approximately 100,000 MOFs are known, with potential applications ranging from gas storage and chemical separation to pollution control.

Turning these materials into functional devices requires precise fabrication, often involving dry etching, which removes material using energetic particles such as ions. Unfortunately, ion beams can disrupt the delicate crystalline frameworks and produce unwanted cavities. Cryogenic etching has offered a way to limit this damage, but it requires specialized cooling equipment and liquid nitrogen.

Led by Assistant Professor Yumeng Zheng and Professor Kentaro Kinoshita from TUS’s Department of Applied Physics, the researchers investigated whether ionic liquids could make MOFs more resistant to ion beam damage. Their approach builds on earlier findings from Kinoshita’s team showing that these liquids can improve the mechanical stability of MOFs. The study was scheduled for publication in Communications Materials.

The team tested four imidazolium-based ionic liquids in Cu3BTC2, a copper-based MOF containing benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (BTC). Each liquid occupied approximately 50% to 60% of the material’s pore volume. The researchers then used a focused gallium ion beam to etch patterns into the samples at room temperature.

Untreated MOFs suffered substantial structural damage, including the formation of large cavities. Samples containing ionic liquids showed considerably less visible microstructural damage under the same conditions. The researchers successfully etched a square measuring 5 × 5 micrometers (approximately 0.0002 × 0.0002 inches), a pillar, and a Chinese character with lines just 130 to 300 nanometers (about 5 to 12 millionths of an inch) wide.

“In this study, we developed a simple method for room-temperature dry etching of this fragile class of materials. By infiltrating MOFs with ionic liquids, their mechanical stability is greatly improved, and the damage from electron and ion beams is reduced, achieving harmless ion beam etching,” says Dr. Zheng.

The researchers propose that ionic liquids protect MOFs through a combination of thermal and electrical effects. The liquids may absorb heat generated during ion bombardment, reducing local temperature changes, while their mobile ions could help redistribute accumulated electrical charge and screen local electric fields. These mechanisms remain proposed explanations rather than directly established causes of the reduced damage.

Additional measurements confirmed that all four ionic liquid treatments increased the MOF’s hardness without substantially changing its stiffness. Thermal analysis also showed that treated samples decomposed at higher temperatures than untreated material, indicating improved thermal stability.

Although the experiments focused on a single copper-based MOF, the researchers believe the approach could potentially work with other frameworks. If its effectiveness extends to additional materials, room-temperature etching could provide a more accessible route to manufacturing MOF-based devices without the cooling requirements of cryogenic processing.

“We can foresee applications in high-sensitivity sensors, separation and analysis devices, and catalytic devices. This technology has the potential to become a foundational technology for bridging the exceptional material functionalities of MOFs with their use in practical devices,” says Prof. Kinoshita.

Reference: “Ionic-liquid-assisted room-temperature dry etching of metal–organic frameworks” by Yumeng Zheng, Momoka Muraoka, Koki Egawa and Kentaro Kinoshita, 10 November 2026, Communications Materials. DOI: 10.1038/s43246-026-01396-3

This work was partly supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 26K00987.

#6274. Experts who study AI in classrooms ranked what matters most, and it isn’t the technology

Seventy experts from 18 countries rated 15 trends in AI in education, and teaching AI skills to both students and teachers came out at the top of the list.

Most conversations around integrating AI in classrooms focus on flashy new tech, like AI tutors for every student or programs that grade homework overnight.

But according to 70 specialists from 18 different countries, the most critical AI trend for the next three years has nothing to do with buying new software.

Their number one priority is basic AI literacy. Both students and teachers need to be taught what these tools are actually doing and when to question their answers.

Rwitajit Majumdar of Kumamoto University in Japan led the study. Colleagues at Dublin City University, Griffith University, the University of Twente, and universities in Germany and Finland joined him.

It’s an expert survey, not a trial in classrooms, so its answers are the panel’s judgment rather than measured results.

The team used a Delphi process, which is a way of drawing a consensus out of experts in rounds. First, 17 researchers submitted 56 trends in AI and education. The team grouped those into 15 themes, from virtual teaching assistants to automated grading to equal access.

Then 70 people rated each theme from 1 to 10 on three questions. How important will it be for learning and teaching within three years? How much impact will it have? And how hard will it be to get right?

Twenty-six of the raters came from academia and 23 from research. Eight worked in policy, eight were teachers, and five came from industry. Germany and Ireland between them supplied 31 of the 70.

The ratings were then argued over in person. About 130 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners met in Dublin in June 2025 at EDUsummIT, a gathering endorsed by UNESCO.

In small groups, each participant took on the role of a teacher, a developer, a researcher, or a policymaker and argued from that seat.

AI-related competences for learners and educators scored highest on both impact, at 8.57 out of 10, and importance, at 8.64.

The panel rated it moderately hard to achieve, at 7.49. That left it with a positive balance of payoff to difficulty, which the authors read as strong consensus that competence comes first.

Two themes tied for second on impact, at 8.13 each. One was automated assessment and feedback, the AI tutor that marks work and responds to each student. The other was the changing role of the teacher who works alongside such tools.

The two parted ways on difficulty. The experts rated automated feedback a moderate challenge, at 7.13. They rated the teacher’s new role one of the hardest things on the list, at 8.40, which the authors read as high impact and high complexity at once.

Two more themes rounded out the top five. One was whether an AI system can explain itself and be trusted, with an impact score of 7.84. The other was whether every student gets equal access to it, at 7.81.

Both drew challenge scores above 8. The authors read those as barriers in ethics, infrastructure, and policy rather than in the technology itself.

Two cheaper wins also stood out in the panel’s arithmetic. AI-assisted content creation and AI for administrative paperwork both paired high importance with lower difficulty, which the authors flagged as candidates for near-term action.

The themes at the bottom were the most technical ones and were also rated as hard. This made them the least urgent.

Linking AI to classroom devices such as virtual reality headsets scored 5.39 on impact. Software that connects AI to a school’s older data systems scored 5.60, and AI-built maps linking subjects across the curriculum scored 5.90.

Across all 15 themes, the panel’s average importance score was 7.31. That sat slightly above its average impact and challenge scores, but the three didn’t differ in any reliable way.

The experts saw AI in education as roughly as hard as it is promising.

A consensus method can narrow the range of views it reports, the authors wrote. The 70 experts were also a convenience sample rather than a representative one.

Furthermore, no students and no parents took part, though they are the people for whom the systems are built.

The ratings forecast three years ahead. Whether the themes the panel ranked highest turn out to be the ones that matter in real classrooms hasn’t been checked.

The authors called for larger panels in each region, with students and parents included, and for work that goes beyond ranking priorities to testing them.

The full study was published in the journal Computers and Education Open.

#6273. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6272. Powerful New Weight-Loss Drug Could Change How Millions Treat Painful Knee Arthritis

An experimental weight-loss injection may offer more than a way to shed pounds, with clinical trials suggesting it could also ease the burden of painful knee arthritis.

Losing weight can help relieve knee osteoarthritis, yet the condition often makes weight loss difficult in the first place. When walking, climbing stairs, or simply standing up from a chair causes pain, getting enough exercise can become a challenge.

For the roughly 15 million Americans living with painful knee osteoarthritis, treatment options remain limited. Physical therapy, topical medications, anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren, opioids, and corticosteroid injections can help manage symptoms, although steroid injections typically provide only short-term relief.

Previous research has shown that losing just 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can improve symptoms. Losing more than 10%, however, is difficult through lifestyle changes alone, particularly for people whose knees already limit their movement.

An experimental weight-loss injection called retatrutide may offer another way to address this problem. In two large clinical trials led by Northwestern University, participants who were overweight or had obesity experienced substantial weight loss alongside significant reductions in knee pain.

The phase 3 trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, involved more than 1,000 participants combined. Those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost approximately 25% of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that about two-thirds of participants receiving the drug reported at least a 50% reduction in knee pain, compared with 38% of those given a placebo.

Researchers tracked these changes using the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC), which asks patients to rate their pain from 0 to 10. Participants also recorded their daily pain levels through an app.

“The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you’re going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain,” said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “A major factor is that you’re loading your knees less and therefore, there’s less pain and it allows you to increase your function.”

Developed by Eli Lilly, retatrutide is a once-weekly injection that activates receptors for three naturally occurring hormones involved in metabolism. Existing weight-loss medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide target one or two receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%. Retatrutide produced losses of approximately 20% to 25% in these trials.

“Participants had remarkable responses,” Schnitzer said. “Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.”

The improvements also extended beyond body weight and joint pain. Participants experienced lower blood pressure, reduced blood lipid levels, and less systemic inflammation, suggesting broader metabolic benefits.

Scientists from Eli Lilly were among the study’s co-authors. Philip Conaghan, professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from the TRIUMPH-4 trial at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were presented separately during a poster session.

Despite the promising results, retatrutide remains experimental and would require approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before becoming a treatment option. Schnitzer emphasized that diet, exercise, and lifestyle changes should remain the first approach because they are less expensive and avoid potential side effects associated with GLP-1 medications, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss. Preserving muscle is especially important for patients with knee osteoarthritis because it helps stabilize the joint.

The trials also left a crucial question unanswered. Although retatrutide significantly reduced pain, researchers do not yet know whether it slows the underlying progression of osteoarthritis or could help patients avoid knee replacement surgery. People who already needed knee replacements were excluded from the studies.

“That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people’s pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis,” Schnitzer said.

Further research must also determine whether retatrutide could benefit people with knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight, since they were not included in the trials. Scientists are particularly interested in whether the drug’s potential anti-inflammatory effects contribute to pain relief independently of weight loss.

“These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known,” Schnitzer said. “Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I’ve been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.”

Reference: “Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity” by Thomas J. Schnitzer, David J. Hunter, Philip G. Conaghan, Arya M. Sharma, Sue D. Pedersen, Kaiyi Chen, So Young Park, Nune Makarova, Kathryn Giblin and Tammy Forrester, 7 November 2026, New England Journal of Medicine. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa2610676

Funding for the study was provided by Eli Lilly and Company.

#6271. Scientists learn why a sensitive part of our DNA is actually a built-in shield against the sun

Under early-Earth ultraviolet light, thymine broke faster than uracil but steered the damage toward lesions that can be undone.

Before Earth had an ozone layer to block the sun, early life was constantly blasted by intense ultraviolet light. Because of this, scientists were puzzled by why DNA evolved using a chemical building block called thymine. It takes significantly more UV damage than similar molecules.

Thymine initially looked like a big evolutionary mistake. But new measurements reveal a clever survival trick.

The specific damage thymine takes from UV light is incredibly easy to undo. Instead of being a weak point, thymine actually takes the hit so the rest of the DNA stays safe.

Peter Rentzepis and two members of his lab at Texas A&M University, Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar, exposed both letters to the same ultraviolet light and tracked what broke.

Thymine fell apart faster overall, but it formed the permanent kind of lesion more slowly than uracil did.

“We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form,” said Khosh Abady, a research assistant in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

He added that this suggests early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight by controlling the damage and making it easier to repair, not by avoiding the damage.

RNA and DNA each spell their code with four letters, and three are shared. RNA uses uracil. DNA uses thymine, which is uracil with one small carbon group attached.

Thymine absorbs ultraviolet light most strongly at 265 nanometers, and uracil at 259. A six-nanometer shift matters on a planet with no ozone layer.

Models of the early Sun suggest the light reaching the surface was about 2.5 times more intense at thymine’s peak than at uracil’s. Thymine’s absorption band is also about 9 percent wider.

On paper, life swapped in the letter that catches more of the most damaging light.

The team dissolved each letter in water and froze the solutions at 5°F (-15°C) in quartz cells. Then they shone a narrow ultraviolet LED on them at 265 nanometers.

Freezing pushes the molecules out of the growing ice into crowded pockets, which mimics how letters sit side by side in a strand, where the main lesions form between neighbors.

Over an hour of exposure, the team tracked three things. They measured how much light the molecules absorbed and how much they glowed.

They also recorded each sample’s Raman spectrum, a fingerprint of chemical bonds that shifts as bonds break and form.

Judged by how fast its absorption faded, thymine degraded in ultraviolet light nearly three times as fast as uracil. It also glowed about 4.5 times more brightly.

The team reads the glow as a sign that excited thymine lingers longer before settling down, which leaves more time for reactions.

Ultraviolet light produces two main lesions between neighboring letters. In one, two letters lock together in a small ring. The team classifies this lesion as reversible, since it can come apart again without enzymes.

In the other, the letters bond in a way that rearranges them for good.

Thymine formed the permanent kind at a rate of 1.56 per minute in the team’s fitted curves, against 2.04 for uracil. So thymine took more damage but steered it toward the repairable kind.

The authors wrote that the letters appear to have been selected to keep damage confined and reversible, not to avoid it. Repair enzymes did not yet exist.

“In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule,” Khosh Abady said.

The experiment used single letters packed in ice, not strands of DNA or RNA in water. The authors wrote that the frozen setup does not capture the full chemistry of real genetic molecules.

The 2.5-fold difference in early sunlight is a modeled figure that depends on the atmosphere assumed.

A separate test, published this month, found that life’s letters were not consistently tougher under ultraviolet light than alternatives that life does not use. So the sunscreen idea is one explanation among several.

There is also a later, better-known reason for thymine. Cytosine, another DNA letter, slowly decays into uracil on its own, and a cell that used uracil as a normal letter could not tell that mistake from the real thing.

That defense needs repair enzymes, so the authors place it after the sunlight pressure, as a reinforcement rather than the origin.

The measured signatures of thymine and uracil, before and after damage, have a second use.

The team wrote that the data could help read ultraviolet damage in whole cells, which would show whether a water-treatment lamp has actually inactivated microbes.

Next, the lab plans to look earlier in the story. The open question is what brought the letters together in the first place, and whether some arrived on meteorites rather than forming on Earth.

The full study was published in the journal PNAS.

#6270. Ancient European Trees Just Solved a 3,500-Year-Old Cold Case: When Did Babylon Fall?

It’s a detective story jam-packed with historical ramifications.

Mesopotamia in the second millennium B.C.E. left behind an unusually rich written record. Yet historians still can’t agree on exact dates. Rival chronologies hinge on when Babylon fell, and they disagree about that by more than a century, so it’s hard to line up events across the Near East and eastern Mediterranean.

Babylon may be best known today from sacred texts, from the Hebrew Bible to the Quran. But long before those books were written, the fabled city on the Euphrates was the capital of one of the ancient world’s great powers. It was home to King Hammurabi, whose law code ranks among the oldest written legal systems on record.

On paper, Mesopotamia should be easy to date. Scribes left behind king lists, administrative records, and royal inscriptions that lay out what happened and in what order. The catch is that they counted time by kings’ reigns, not calendar years, so the whole sequence had no fixed link to dates we’d recognize.

Venus should have fixed that. Babylonian scribes watched the sky for omens, believing the planets’ movements foretold harvests, wars, and the fate of the king. During the reign of King Ammisaduqa, they wrote down when Venus appeared and disappeared on the horizon, dating each sighting by year of his reign. Because Ammisaduqa also appears in the king lists, those sightings tie the whole sequence of kings to the sky, and modern astronomers can work out when they could have happened.

The trouble is that Venus repeats itself, so the observations fit several possible points in history. That left four rival timelines (high, middle, low, and ultra-low) that place Babylon’s fall as much as 150 years apart.

The key witness turned out to be wood. Timbers from ancient buildings in Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey, had tree rings that could be lined up in order, but no one could pin that sequence to actual calendar years. Yet those same sites are tied to Mesopotamia through the Old Assyrian trade network, whose merchants left records that line up with Mesopotamian kings. So dating the wood would date the history, too.

Now, researchers believe they’ve done just that. In a study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team wrote that they used “patterns captured in single-year radiocarbon measurements from tree rings to calendar-date Anatolian wood samples from sites with direct archaeological links to Mesopotamia.”

Led by Charlotte Pearson of the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona, the team measured carbon-14 in single annual growth rings from the Anatolian timbers. They partnered with ETH Zurich’s Laboratory of Ion Beam Physics to make the measurements.

To anchor the Anatolian wood, the team turned to precisely dated Tyrolean stone pine from Austria and oak from Germany. That pinned the Anatolian tree-ring sequence to the calendar, with each ring now tied to a specific year from 2072 to 744 B.C.E. The payoff reaches beyond Mesopotamia. “These data can now be used for samples from anywhere else in the world,” Kurt Nicolussi of the University of Innsbruck told Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF, in a translated report.

“Tree-ring dates are combined with archaeological and high-resolution ice-core evidence to evaluate the competing chronological frameworks for Mesopotamia between 2000 and 1500 B.C.E.,” the authors wrote.

The verdict: The Old Babylonian Empire fell in 1587 B.C.E. The authors found “strong support” for what they call a middle-low chronology, a timeline that falls between the middle and low models.

“This illustrates how high-precision radiocarbon methods, in combination with other interdisciplinary evidence, can enhance chronological accuracy across many time periods,” the authors wrote.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.
