#6261. Why do people keep stealing? Scientists uncover new clues

A study of repeat theft offenders suggests that difficulty learning from rewards may help explain why some people keep stealing.

People who repeatedly steal for profit may struggle to learn from rewards, a new study suggests.

In a game about finding the best payoff, offenders without kleptomania were slower to learn which choices paid off than people with no criminal record.

Yukiori Goto of the Graduate School of Informatics at Kyoto University in Japan led the research.

Among the co-authors are a clinician who treats kleptomania and a researcher at the Training Institute for Correctional Personnel of the Japanese Ministry of Justice.

The game tested only how people learn from rewards (not how they respond to punishment). Further, each person was tested once, so the study shows a difference between groups but cannot say what caused it.

According to Goto’s team, many people continue stealing even after being punished or sent to prison.

Some have kleptomania, a mental health condition that causes a strong urge to steal things, even when they have little or no value.

Others steal for money, out of need, or because of antisocial behavior. This is known as instrumental theft.

The study included 50 repeat theft offenders in Japan, most of whom had been jailed for shoplifting. Of these, 12 had kleptomania and were receiving treatment, while 38 did not have the condition.

Researchers compared both groups with 53 people who had no criminal record.

Each person played a computer game with four colored options on the screen. Each choice produced a payoff (a number from 1 to 100), and players were told to collect as much as they could.

However, the payoffs kept changing. The options started with average payoffs ranging from 20 to 80, and each payoff rose or fell from one round to the next.

Thus, the option that paid best at the start might not remain the best. A player had to keep deciding whether to make the same choice again or try another option.

The game ran for 160 rounds, and players had 1.5 seconds to choose or the payoff of that round was lost.

The game was shorter than in earlier research. Many participants, particularly the theft offenders, had dropped out of longer trial runs.

Compared with people who had no criminal record, the 38 offenders without kleptomania chose the best-paying option less often. The gap between their winnings and the best possible total was larger too.

Next, the choices of each person were fitted to a mathematical model of how people learn from rewards (a process known as reinforcement learning).

In the model, the learning rate describes how much each new payoff changes a player’s estimate of what an option is worth.

After age, sex, and smoking were accounted for, the offenders without kleptomania had a lower learning rate than the people with no criminal record.

By the team’s statistics, the data were about 650 times more likely with a real difference in learning rate between those two groups than without one.

“Given that instrumental theft is a profit-seeking behavior, reinforcement learning has been superficially believed to play a critical role, or even be abnormally enhanced in these individuals,” Goto said.

“Yet our findings have clearly demonstrated that recurrent instrumental theft involves neurobehavioral deficits.”

According to the authors, a person with a low learning rate gives little weight to recent results and is slow to change behavior when payoffs change.

Goto’s team hypothesized that slow learning could stop a person from coming to value stable rewards (such as holding a job). That person may then return to familiar behavior such as theft.

Results for the 12 offenders with kleptomania were inconclusive.

The learning rate in this group appeared higher than in the offenders without kleptomania.

However, the evidence was weak, as the data were only about twice as likely with a real difference between the two offender groups as without one.

The weak evidence may be explained by small group size, the authors wrote, and a larger sample might yet show a learning deficit.

Goto’s team suggested that kleptomania may involve an overwhelming urge to steal or a failure of self-control, rather than trouble learning the value of an action.

Brain signals were recorded from two of the groups as they played (the offenders without kleptomania and the people with no criminal record). The kleptomania group was not recorded, because of practical constraints at the testing sites.

Changes in blood oxygen were measured with near-infrared light at 10 points across the prefrontal cortex, a part of the brain that helps track what actions are worth.

In some parts of the prefrontal cortex, the oxygen signal tracked the value a player expected from the chosen option.

There was no reliable difference between the two groups in how closely the oxygen signal was tied to those values.

In two areas of the right prefrontal cortex, the groups did differ in their baseline oxygen signal, whatever was happening in the game.

Goto’s team suggested that such a baseline difference could add noise to learning signals without changing how the brain tracks value.

Criminal justice systems assume that offenders can adjust their behavior in response to severe consequences, Goto’s team wrote.

The game, which measured learning from rewards only, could not test that assumption.

According to the authors, learning from losses or punishment may work in entirely different ways in people with antisocial traits. The results cannot show how these offenders respond to legal penalties.

Why did these offenders learn more slowly? The researchers suggested two possible reasons: psychopathic or antisocial traits, or time spent in prison or other institutions.

Future studies could track offenders after release and test how they learn from punishment to see whether slow learning affects real-life stealing.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology.

#6260. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#6259. Which Kindle Should You Buy? We Break Down Each Model

Here's what to know about the newest models and which ones are worth buying.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There's something about reading on a Kindle that makes it easier to get through your reading list. Instead of carrying a stack of books or getting distracted by phone notifications, you can keep thousands of titles in one lightweight e-reader. Whether you're reading on your commute, relaxing by the pool, or finishing one more chapter before bed, a Kindle makes it easy to take your library wherever you go.

And Amazon's latest lineup gives readers even more reasons to make the switch. In October 2026, the company introduced a completely redesigned collection of Kindles, including updated versions of its entry-level Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new devices feature thinner and lighter designs, flush-front displays, and faster performance. Amazon also introduced its first aluminum Kindle, giving its smallest e-reader a more premium feel, along with new colors like Ube, Alpine Sky, and Seaglass Green.

The differences between the models go beyond their designs. The standard Kindle is still an excellent option for readers who want something small and affordable, while the Paperwhite offers a larger display that comes with adjustable warm lighting and waterproof protection. For readers who prefer graphic novels and illustrated books, the Colorsoft brings color to an E Ink display. And if you're interested in taking notes or marking up documents, Amazon's Kindle Scribe lineup offers an entirely different experience.

With so many models to choose from, finding the right Kindle ultimately comes down to how and where you like to read. We've broken down the best Kindles available right now, so read on to find the one that's right for you.

The Kindle Paperwhite continues to hit the sweet spot between features, portability, and price. Amazon's newest version is thinner and lighter than its predecessor, with a redesigned 7-inch display that offers exceptionally sharp text and improved contrast. It's comfortable enough to hold for extended reading sessions while offering more screen space than the standard Kindle.

It also has adjustable warm light, letting you shift the display's tone from white to amber for more comfortable nighttime reading. The waterproof design makes it a great choice for reading by the pool or in the bathtub, while its battery can last up to 12 weeks on a single charge. For most readers, the Paperwhite offers everything they need without the higher price of Amazon's premium models.

Amazon's entry-level Kindle has always been a great option for readers who value portability, and the latest version makes an even stronger case for choosing the smaller model. With a 6-inch display, it's the most pocket-friendly Kindle in the lineup, making it particularly convenient for commuting, traveling, or reading on the go.

Amazon redesigned the device with a thinner body and a flush-front display for a more modern look. Books also open 30 percent faster than on the previous model. The 300 PPI display keeps text sharp, and the battery lasts up to six weeks on a charge. You won't get the Paperwhite's waterproof protection or adjustable warm light, but for readers who simply want an easy way to carry their favorite books, the standard Kindle is an excellent choice.

The standard Kindle gets a premium makeover with Amazon's first aluminum version. It keeps the same compact 6-inch display as the entry-level model but replaces the traditional exterior with a sleek, matte aluminum back made with 80 percent recycled aluminum. The result is a more refined e-reader that still fits easily into a pocket or small bag.

Another advantage is the additional storage. The aluminum Kindle comes with 32GB, double the capacity of the standard version, and doesn't include lock-screen advertisements. It's also offered in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green, making it one of the more visually distinctive Kindles available. If you like the portability of the smallest Kindle but want something that feels a little more premium, this version is worth the upgrade.

The Paperwhite Signature Edition takes everything that makes the standard Paperwhite great and adds a few premium features. Like its more affordable counterpart, it has a sharp 7-inch display, waterproof protection, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. However, it also comes with an aluminum rear housing, 32GB of storage, and an auto-adjusting front light that responds to your surroundings.

The latest version adds double-tap page turning, letting you advance through your book with a simple gesture. It also supports charging through a compatible pogo-pin dock (sold separately) or the USB-C port. None of these features are essential for enjoying a book, but they make the reading experience more convenient. For anyone who spends hours reading every week, the Signature Edition offers a particularly polished experience.

If you frequently read comics, graphic novels, travel guides, or other illustrated books, the Kindle Colorsoft makes a compelling case for upgrading from a traditional black-and-white e-reader. Its 7-inch color E Ink display brings book covers, photographs, and illustrations to life while maintaining the paper-like appearance that makes Kindles comfortable to read.

Amazon redesigned the latest Colorsoft with improved display technology intended to provide richer color, better contrast, and more consistent illumination. It also has adjustable warm lighting and waterproof protection, making it versatile enough for reading at home or while traveling. The battery lasts up to eight weeks, which is less than the Paperwhite but still impressive compared to most tablets. For readers who want to see their books in color without sacrificing the distraction-free Kindle experience, the Colorsoft is an excellent option.

The Colorsoft Signature Edition is Amazon's most feature-packed dedicated reading Kindle. It combines the standard Colorsoft color E Ink display with additional features designed to make everyday reading easier, including an auto-adjusting front light, double-tap page turning, and charging through a compatible dock.

Its aluminum housing gives it a premium look and feel, while the 32GB of storage provides plenty of room for books, audiobooks, comics, and graphic novels. It also comes in Graphite and Fig, the latter offering a more colorful alternative to the traditional black e-reader. Readers who primarily enjoy text-based novels probably don't need to spend extra for these upgrades. But if you frequently read illustrated content and want Amazon's best color-reading features in a compact Kindle, the Signature Edition is a strong choice.

For young readers who gravitate toward graphic novels, comics, and illustrated stories, the Kindle Colorsoft Kids offers a more engaging way to read. Its 7-inch color E Ink display brings illustrations and book covers to life without the distracting apps, videos, and games found on traditional tablets.

The newest version also features an adjustable warm light, waterproof protection, and up to eight weeks of battery life. Parents get access to Amazon's parental controls, while the included one-year Kids+ subscription provides plenty of books to explore. The Colorsoft Kids costs considerably more than the other children's Kindles, but its color display makes it especially appealing for young readers who enjoy books where illustrations are as important as the words.

The newest full-featured Kindle Scribe is much more than a traditional e-reader. With an expansive 11-inch display and an included Premium Pen, it doubles as a digital notebook for jotting down ideas, taking meeting notes, reviewing documents, and annotating books. The redesigned device is thinner and lighter than previous generations, with faster writing and page turns that make the experience feel more natural.

Amazon also introduced productivity features that set the Scribe apart from its smaller e-readers. You can import documents from supported cloud services, organize notebooks, and use AI-powered tools to search and summarize notes. The built-in front light makes it practical for reading and writing in different lighting conditions. While the larger size and higher price won't appeal to everyone, the Scribe is one of Amazon's most versatile devices for readers who also enjoy writing.

Amazon's Kindles come in several screen sizes, and choosing the right one depends largely on how and where you read. The standard Kindle has a compact 6-inch display that's particularly convenient for commuting and traveling. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft models increase the screen size to 7 inches, offering more room for text and illustrations without becoming significantly less portable.

For readers who want to write notes or work with documents, the Kindle Scribe models have much larger 11-inch displays. They're better suited for desk use or studying, though their size makes them less convenient to carry around.

Most Kindles use black-and-white E Ink displays, which are ideal for traditional books and text-based reading. However, the Colorsoft and Scribe Colorsoft offer color displays that can make a noticeable difference when reading comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, or documents with colorful charts.

If you primarily read novels, there's little reason to spend extra for a color display. However, readers who enjoy illustrated content may appreciate the additional versatility.

The standard Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft each offer 16GB of storage, which is more than enough for thousands of traditional e-books. Signature Edition models and the aluminum Kindle increase that capacity to 32GB, while select Scribe models offer up to 64GB.

Battery life is also impressive across the lineup. The newest standard Kindle offers up to six weeks on a single charge, while the Paperwhite can last up to 12 weeks. The Colorsoft models promise up to eight weeks, depending on usage. For the Scribe lineup, battery life depends on whether you're primarily reading or writing with the included stylus; frequent note-taking uses more power.

Amazon's more expensive Kindles offer features that can make reading more convenient, including waterproof protection, adjustable warm lighting, and auto-adjusting brightness. The new Paperwhite Signature Edition and Colorsoft Signature Edition also support double-tap page turning and charging through an optional dock.

For many readers, these upgrades aren't necessary. However, they're worth considering if you frequently read at night, take your Kindle near water, or want a more premium device that you'll use every day.

#6258. Young people worry about climate change, so what holds them back from taking action?

A survey of young Americans explores why climate worry can accompany both a willingness to act and a sense that taking action is pointless.

Worrying about climate change does not always translate into a willingness to act. A new study led by Portland State University suggests why.

Of the 1,603 young Americans who were surveyed, those most worried about the climate were the most willing to act on it.

Yet they were also the likeliest to feel that acting was useless, a state known as eco-paralysis.

But worry was not the strongest sign of eco-paralysis. Feeling annoyed by constant warnings about climate change was.

The study was led by Brianne Suldovsky, an associate professor of communication at Portland State University, together with colleagues at High Point University and the University of Arizona.

Because everyone answered the survey only once, the results can show which feelings tend to occur together, though not whether one of them causes another.

“We often assume that young people who are anxious about climate change will be motivated to do something about it,” Suldovsky said.

“Our findings suggest the relationship is much more complicated. Climate anxiety can motivate action, but it can also contribute to feelings of paralysis.”

The survey ran online for three weeks in late September and early October of 2024. Those who took it were aged between 13 and 22 and lived across the United States, with just under half of them younger than 18.

For most of it they were shown statements and asked to rate, from 1 to 5, how far they agreed with each.

There were nine statements about worry, one of which was “I feel anxious when I think about the consequences of climate change.”

They were also asked how willing they would be to do seven everyday things by themselves, such as recycling or turning the lights off when no one needs them.

Another seven activities involved broader political or collective action.

These included signing a petition, volunteering for a climate organization, and voting for a candidate who supports climate action.

A further 11 statements measured eco-paralysis, including “When I think about climate change, I feel so overwhelmed that I can’t do anything anymore.”

The more worried young people were, the more willing they said they were to act, and worry predicted that willingness better than anything else in the survey.

That was the case for the everyday steps and even more so for the group efforts.

Those who had given climate change more thought beforehand, and who rated it as more important to them personally, were more willing as well.

All of this is in line with what earlier studies of climate anxiety in teenagers and young adults have reported.

Worry also predicted eco-paralysis, though. The more worried a young person was, the more they agreed that their own efforts would not change anything.

Worry by itself could therefore not explain who wanted to act and who felt stuck.

The survey also measured a feeling which the researchers call climate contempt, using four statements that included “I am bored of hearing about climate change” and “I am annoyed by the constant publicity around climate change.”

Of everything that was analyzed, agreement with those four statements predicted eco-paralysis the most strongly, more so than worry did.

The young people who agreed with them more were also less willing either to take the everyday steps or to join the group efforts.

“Importantly, we found that climate contempt – or feeling annoyed about the panic over climate change – may be a key factor in understanding why some young people disengage from climate action altogether,” Suldovsky said.

Worry and annoyance were analyzed side by side, and each had its own link to eco-paralysis. The team did not test whether feeling both at once has any effect of its own.

Those who scored higher on worry tended to score somewhat lower on annoyance.

Asked where they learned about climate change, the young people said they had learned more from social media than from news outlets or from the people around them.

Yet how much they had learned from social media wasn’t tied to willingness to act, and it wasn’t tied to eco-paralysis.

It was different for news media. Those who had learned more from newspapers, TV, radio, online news or podcasts were more willing to join group efforts.

So were those who had learned more from family, friends, classmates and teachers, although that link was weaker. Neither of these sources was tied to the everyday steps such as recycling.

The survey asked only how much people had learned and not what they had learned. The authors noted that social media can carry false information about climate change as well as accurate information.

Close to half of U.S. teens described themselves as online almost constantly in a 2024 report from the Pew Research Center.

The study had several limits. Because it surveyed participants only once, researchers could not tell whether feelings influenced willingness to act or the reverse. It also measured intentions, not actual actions.

All participants had signed up for paid online surveys, so the findings may not reflect all young Americans.

Another concern was how contempt was measured. The questions focused on annoyance, boredom and surprise rather than hostility or resentment.

No climate messages were tested, leaving researchers unable to say which ones might cause annoyance.

Suldovsky’s team called for future experiments to compare climate messages and track what young people actually do, not just what they say they might do.

The full study was published in the journal Climate.

A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.

The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Winterstein, A. G., Chen, H., Thai, T., Wang, Y., Smolinski, N. E., Wen, W., Ewig, C. L., Gilboa, S. M., Meaney-Delman, D., Maro, J. C., & Rasmussen, S. A. (2026). Doxycycline and risk for pregnancy loss: A multi-database, multi-indication cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-01647

#6256. Repairing damaged cells may not be enough to reverse aging

A new theory suggests the body’s signals may amplify cellular damage, helping explain why repairing cells alone might not reverse aging.

Aging is often described as a slow build-up of damage, but it is not a constant process. For many decades, the body declines only slowly, whereas in old age this decline speeds up sharply.

Some forms of cellular damage accumulate at a roughly steady rate in adulthood, yet the risk of death rises much faster. Why is that?

In a new paper, Pierre-Edouard Sottas of the xLongevity Center in Vevey, Switzerland, draws attention to the signals that pass between our cells and organs.

In his view, the effects of cell damage are not necessarily confined to the place where the damage occurs. They may be spread through the body by its own signaling network, and may even be amplified.

Further, if this is correct, simply repairing damaged cells may not be enough to reverse aging in old age.

This is only a theory for now. Sottas did not carry out any new experiments, but built his argument on previous research and a simple mathematical model.

So what is the real question for Sottas? An aging body, in his account, is more than the sum of the defects in its separate cells and tissues.

“The key question is what determines whether local dysfunction stays contained, is buffered, or becomes organism-level decline,” he wrote.

Earlier population analyses estimated that eliminating all cancer deaths would add only a few years to life expectancy, because the people spared would still die of other causes.

The risk of dying of those other causes rises steeply with age. This steep rise in the risk of death was first described in 1825, and is known as the Gompertz law.

Under this law, an adult’s risk of death does not increase by a fixed amount each year, but is multiplied instead. At the rate used by Sottas for humans, the risk doubles about every eight years.

As a result, deaths in late life are not spread evenly, but fall within a fairly narrow window of ages. According to Sottas’s calculation, the typical spread in the age at death is about 15 years.

Cell damage of several kinds, on the other hand, builds up in adults at a roughly constant rate.

Measurements show this for DNA mutations, for the shortening of telomeres (the protective caps on chromosomes) and for changes in the chemical tags on DNA.

On its own, a constant rate of cell damage is not enough to explain a risk of death that keeps doubling, Sottas wrote.

Sottas explains his idea using two terms: “load” and “gain.” Load is the damage that builds up inside cells. Gain is how much the body’s signals increase the effects of that damage.

His idea builds on a theory by Mikhail Blagosklonny, who suggested that the processes helping us grow when we’re young don’t fully switch off. As we age, they can start doing more harm than good.

Sottas believes something similar happens with the body’s immune, inflammatory and hormonal signals. When we’re young, they help protect and repair us.

But as we get older, these signals may keep spreading and making each other stronger.

Think of a microphone too close to a speaker. A small hum quickly turns into a loud screech. Sottas suggests aging signals may work in much the same way.

Cells that have stopped dividing for good (because of damage or stress) are known as senescent cells. In early life, this shutdown serves as a defense against cancer.

However, these cells are not inactive. They release molecules that promote inflammation, and they also release tiny membrane-wrapped packets, called extracellular vesicles, which carry proteins and genetic material.

These signals can reach other cells, nearby and in distant tissues. Those cells can then be pushed into the senescent state too, and start to send out signals of their own.

There are estimated to be 1.5 trillion vesicles entering human blood plasma every minute, which translates to tens of vesicles per day for every cell of the body.

A senescent cell can release vesicles at 10 to 100 times the rate of the non-senescent cells around it. Thus, only a small number of such cells is needed to supply a large share of the signal.

According to Sottas, the loop is held in check in a young body by systems of repair and clean-up.

As these systems weaken with age, senescent cells build up, and even a little new damage can then have an outsized effect on the whole body.

Sottas also addressed the case of the naked mole-rat, an exceptionally long-lived rodent, which he treated as a natural test of the theory.

The cells of the naked mole-rat are not spared from damage. In fact, more oxygen-related damage (to fats, DNA and proteins) has been reported in this animal than in mice, even at young ages. The chemical tags on its DNA also change with age.

If the pace of aging were set by damage alone, then the animal’s risk of death would be expected to rise sharply with age.

But this isn’t the case in the naked mole-rat. Across more than three decades of records, its risk of dying has hardly increased with age at all.

For Sottas, this suggests that the load is present in these animals without the gain. Even though the cells of the naked mole-rat suffer damage, this damage may never be amplified.

Why not? One possible reason comes from experiments on naked mole-rat cells. When these cells were pushed into the senescent state, they went on to die, which could prevent senescent cells from building up and their signals from persisting.

Sottas cited a study in which half the plasma (the liquid part of blood) of old mice was replaced with salt water and albumin, a blood protein. No young blood was added.

Afterward, muscle repair in the old mice improved, their livers had less fat and scarring, and more new nerve cells formed in the brain.

For Sottas, these findings support the idea that reducing circulating signals may improve tissue function in old mice.

Human evidence remains at an early stage. In a placebo-controlled trial of 42 healthy adults (over 50), a similar procedure called plasma exchange lowered estimates of biological age based on chemical tags on DNA.

These estimates do not establish that participants became healthier or would live longer.

Other treatments act on single cells, for example partial reprogramming, which resets a cell’s gene activity toward a younger state. In mice, this has improved retina, muscle and nerve function.

However, no study has documented the rejuvenation of several organs together (liver, kidney, blood vessels, immune system and brain) after such treatment.

According to Sottas, the repair of cells should work best as prevention in early life and may slow aging in midlife.

He proposes that lasting reversal in late life would require resetting the body’s signals.

In his paper, Sottas does not actually show that changing the body’s signals can reverse aging in humans. His model follows only four quantities, and the human evidence comes from two small studies.

Sottas was a co-author of one of them, a pilot that was completed by only 14 healthy volunteers. A comparison group was missing.

He is also affiliated with xLongevity, an organization active in longevity and rejuvenation. Sottas disclosed this as a conflict of interest.

Some damage may also remain even after the signals are reset. A reset might soften the effects of such damage (DNA mutations, shortened telomeres, stiffened collagen), but according to Sottas its full correction may require repairs inside cells.

Sottas has outlined six testable predictions, one of which is that shifts in the signals of the blood should appear before any improvement in the tissues.

The question that is still open is whether a reset of the body’s signals can produce a lasting improvement across many organs.

New methods to measure biological age, which go beyond the chemical tags on DNA, are needed to address this question, Sottas suggested.

The paper was published in the journal Aging.

#6255. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6254. Tiny ocean animals reveal a hidden foundation of marine life

Tiny ocean animals depend on different food sources across the Pacific, revealing important differences in marine food chains.

Microscopic algae form the base of many ocean food chains, but bacteria also play a major role.

In the warm, nutrient-poor tropical Pacific, researchers found that roughly half of the food supporting tiny crustaceans called Calanus copepods could be traced back to bacteria.

Near the Arctic, in the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea, more than half was supplied instead by dinoflagellates, a group of algae.

Calanus is an important food of fish and seabirds, and a change in what feeds it can therefore be passed on to animals higher in the food web.

The study was led by Hyuntae Choi and Kyung-Hoon Shin of Hanyang University ERICA in South Korea; the co-authors include Brian Popp of the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa.

The copepods were collected on cruises between 2015 and 2020.

What the work provides is therefore a comparison among regions at particular moments; it is no record of change in a single place.

Copepods are small crustaceans that drift with ocean currents. They include Calanus, which feed by filtering tiny food particles from the water.

Adults were collected from two research ships, the Isabu and the icebreaker Araon, by means of nets pulled up from a depth of about 660 feet (200 meters).

From the tropical and subtropical Pacific, the sampling sites extended through the subarctic Pacific and the Bering Sea as far as the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea.

Copepod proteins were then broken down in the laboratory into their separate amino acids. Of these, the essential amino acids cannot be made by animals, which must get them from food.

Production of those amino acids by each source at the base of the food web yields its own mixture of carbon isotopes (slightly heavier and lighter forms of the same element).

Because passage up the food chain leaves the mixture almost unchanged, it serves as a fingerprint.

The proportion derived from each of six groups was then estimated with a statistical model; the groups included diatoms, dinoflagellates, two kinds of cyanobacteria (bacteria that use sunlight) and bacteria that feed on organic matter.

Such proportions refer to the origin of the food and not to what each copepod actually ate, since part of it may first have passed through other microbes.

The tropical Pacific is strongly layered: a warm surface layer mixes little with the nutrient-rich water below it. The condition is known as stratification, and relatively few algae grow there.

Satellite measurements of chlorophyll, the pigment with which algae capture sunlight, ranged there from 0.03 to 0.13 milligrams per cubic meter, against as much as 7.86 near the Bering Strait.

For these tropical waters, the model put about 31% of the copepods’ food base down to bacteria that feed on organic matter.

Cyanobacteria that turn nitrogen gas into a usable nutrient added about 20%, and algae about 47%.

Bacteria thus supplied roughly as much of the food base of tropical copepods as algae did.

Farther north, the share from algae increased with latitude, reaching about 74% in the southern Chukchi Sea.

The share of bacteria feeding on organic matter fell to about 16%, and that of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria to about 7%.

The greater contribution from algae came mainly from dinoflagellates, single-celled organisms that use sunlight and of which some also eat other microbes.

In the tropics, dinoflagellates and diatoms contributed similar shares, about 19% and 18%. In the southern Chukchi Sea, dinoflagellates reached about 52%, whereas diatoms stayed near 15%.

The small share of diatoms is notable, because diatoms were the most common algae counted in the northern water samples (although at some sites dinoflagellates were equally or more numerous).

The ships reached these waters after the bloom of algae had ended, when nutrients were scarce and the sea ice had largely melted.

Dinoflagellates and other small algae tend to become more common under those conditions, the authors noted.

The researchers suggested that diatoms may be digested more slowly, or that copepods may choose other food. Across all sites, the dinoflagellate share increased with chlorophyll, a relationship shown by no other food source.

Nitrogen in the same amino acids was also used to estimate the number of feeding steps between the copepods and the bottom of their food web.

One estimate counts mainly the steps through animals. A second also counts steps through protists, single-celled grazers that eat bacteria and algae.

In the tropics, the second estimate exceeded the first by less than one step. At subarctic and Arctic sites, it exceeded the first by more than one step.

The authors wrote that the larger difference indicates more feeding on protists at higher latitudes during summer.

The difference between the estimates was also greater where the dinoflagellate share was higher.

The team therefore proposed that dinoflagellates able both to use sunlight and to eat microbes may be an important link between microbes and Calanus in the north.

Algae need nitrogen, which here came from two main sources: nitrate dissolved in seawater, or nitrogen gas turned by cyanobacteria into living tissue.

The two sources carry distinct nitrogen isotope signatures, which allowed the contribution of each to be estimated.

In the tropical Pacific, about 29% of the nitrogen in algae was estimated to come from nitrogen gas. Bacteria break down what the cyanobacteria make, and the nitrogen released is taken up by the algae.

In the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea, by contrast, nitrate supplied an estimated 91% of the algae’s nitrogen.

The authors linked the tropical pattern to stratification, which limits the amount of nitrate reaching the sunlit surface where algae grow.

“Importantly, our study shows how warming-driven changes in stratification and nutrient dynamics are reshaping planktonic food webs,” Shin said.

The study nevertheless compared different regions and did not follow a single region as it warmed.

Warm Pacific water flowing north through the Bering Strait in summer has sped up the loss of sea ice in the western Arctic Ocean, the authors noted.

Between 2015 and 2017, no year-to-year differences were found in the diets of copepods from the subarctic Pacific to the southern Chukchi Sea.

Summer surface water in the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea was, however, warmer in 2019 and 2020 than in 2016 through 2018.

An Arctic species, Calanus glacialis, also became less common there, while Pacific species increased.

The authors wrote that food-chain measurements from those warmer years may differ from the ones reported.

Not every copepod was identified to species, and tropical and northern waters were sampled in different months, so that seasonal changes could not be checked.

It also remains unclear whether dinoflagellates that eat other microbes carry the carbon pattern of an alga or that of their prey, an uncertainty that could blur the fingerprints.

The authors called for isotope measurements across more of the North Pacific and over more years, to see how these food chains vary as the ocean keeps warming.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6253. The 8 Best Cheap Washing Machines for Fresh Laundry on a Budget

If you don’t mind skipping the bells and whistles, these affordable appliances—all priced under $1,000—get the job done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You can get by without a washing machine, especially if you live near a laundromat, though you can’t beat the luxury of having one in your basement.

Many of today’s high-end washers have price tags in the thousands, but if you’re shopping on a budget, the good news is that you can find cheap washing machines that cost much less and work just as well.

Whether you want a full-size washing machine to handle your family’s oversized loads or a more compact model that can be tucked in a closet, there are a number of highly rated appliances well under $1,000. Some even have high-end features that are generally reserved for more expensive machines, such as a built-in water faucet or sanitization cycle, which helps make laundry day quicker and easier than ever.

For more of the best washing machines available today, check out our top picks for front-loading washers, top-loading washers, and all-in-one washer-dryers.

To offer a selection of cheap washing machines that will work for every home and budget, we looked for the top products in each of the categories outlined above—full-size, portable, and manual—and only included highly rated models that cost less than $1,000. All the products have a rating of three stars or higher, and we prioritized washing machines from well-regarded brands with good customer service and warranties.

For our most recent update, we reviewed current pricing and availability across major retailers, replaced outdated models, and added new picks based on what offers the best features for different situations. We also consulted with Amy Chernoff at AJ Madison to make sure our buying advice reflects how today’s budget washers compare to their pricier counterparts.

A full-size, high-efficiency washing machine for under $700 isn’t easy to find, but this model from Whirlpool checks all the boxes. The top-loading machine has a 3.5-cubic-foot capacity, and it uses a dual-action spiral agitator to deeply clean your clothing.

This popular washing machine comes with a wide selection of cycles and settings to customize each load. It has options for quick washes, delicates, and bulky items, as well as an auto-sensing feature that uses just the right amount of water for each load.

If all you want is a dependable full-size washer for the least money, this Amana is where I’d start. The high-efficiency agitator and wash system dig into everyday dirt and stains, and I like that the stainless steel wash basket won’t chip or rust over the years the way porcelain-tubs can. When you need to fully soak a bulky load like towels or a comforter, the Deep Water Wash option fills the tub to the max instead of leaving you stuck with an auto-sensed water level.

There’s also an automatic fabric softener dispenser that releases at the right point in the cycle, plus a Quick Wash for small, lightly soiled loads. And thanks to the Late Lid Lock, you get extra time to toss in a stray sock or forgotten shirt before the spin cycle kicks in.

The trade-off is no Wi-Fi, no app, and no sanitize cycle. For a no-frills workhorse that just gets laundry clean, though, those are easy features to give up.

This Samsung washing machine packs an impressive number of features, including a quick wash cycle that completes a full load in under 30 minutes. It has an extra-large 5.2-cubic-foot drum that can easily handle king-size comforters and bulky loads, and a built-in faucet at the back of the tub for pretreating stains before starting a cycle.

Unlike most washers in this price range, Samsung includes Wi-Fi connectivity and smart home integration, so you can remotely start, stop, and schedule loads and get end-of-cycle alerts on your phone. It also works with Alexa and Google Assistant.

Other features include a soft-close lid, a manual water-level override for filling the tub higher than the automatic sensor would, and Energy Star certification, which many budget washers lack. The only notable omission is a steam cycle, but that’s a minor trade-off at this price.

At 4.5 cubic feet, this GE model has a drum that’s big enough to wash a comforter or a week’s worth of clothes for a small family. Similar to the Amana, this GE washer uses a dual-action agitator, where the top half moves independently from the bottom to guide clothes through the water while the lower section agitates along the bottom of the basket. That two-piece design circulates clothes more evenly than a single-piece agitator, which tends to push everything in one direction.

Stainless steel lines the tub instead of porcelain-coated plastic, so chipping and rust spots aren’t a concern down the road. You can also manually control the water level up to 26 gallons—something other high-efficiency washers don’t let you do.

A sanitize cycle hits temperatures high enough to kill 99 percent of bacteria, which is useful for towels, bedding, and sweaty gym clothes. There is no app support, so you can’t start a load remotely or get a notification when a cycle finishes. Instead, you’ll have to listen for the buzzer or set your own timer.

The agitator in this Whirlpool can pop out, setting it apart from other machines on this list. You can remove it when you need to fit something bulky, like a comforter or sleeping bag, then snap it back in for everyday loads. The capacity shifts from 4.2 to 4.3 cubic feet with the agitator removed, and bulky items sit flatter without bunching up around a center post.

In addition to its removable agitator, there are twelve wash cycles that give you several options for different loads. A presoak option lets you loosen stains and wash in a single run instead of soaking separately in a sink or bucket. The sanitize cycle uses higher water temperatures to kill bacteria, which is useful for bedding and gym clothes. A soft-close lid keeps it from slamming every time you load clothes.

While other models on this list let you manually override the water level to fully submerge a bulky comforter or sleeping bag, this Whirlpool relies on auto-sensing only, so you’re stuck with whatever the sensor decides is enough.

Samsung’s front-load washer can easily stack with a matching dryer to cut your laundry footprint roughly in half. It has a depth at just over 31 inches with the door closed, so it can tuck into tighter spaces than a standard front-loader. The drum itself is also 4.5 cubic feet with a stainless steel interior, matching the capacity of the full-size top-loaders on this list.

Samsung’s vibration reduction system dampens noise and movement during spin cycles, which matters if the washer sits on an upper floor or shares a wall with a living space. You can pause a cycle and add a forgotten item through the door—something some front-loaders won’t let you do.

Ten wash cycles cover the basics, plus there’s a prewash and a soak option. However, there’s no sanitizing cycle, so you may have a harder time hitting the higher temperature needed to kill bacteria in towels or bedding.

Other washers push hair around and hope it goes down the drain, which can clog pipes over time. This Maytag model features a built-in filter that catches pet hair during the wash cycle, collecting it so you can clean it out later. The Pet Pro option adds extra water and a deep rinse specifically to work with that filter, so hair actually lifts off fabric instead of reattaching during the spin.

The drum is 4.7 cubic feet with a stainless steel basket and agitator. An Extra Power option adds a pre-wash and extra agitation to any cycle, which helps get rid of stains, rather than pretreating by hand. There’s also a built-in water faucet on the machine itself for spot-treating stains before you start a load.

There are 11 wash cycles, plus an option to add more water when auto-sensing isn’t enough. It’s a good option to have when washing heavy blankets or dog beds that need to be fully submerged. Note, though, that there isn’t a delay start feature, so you can’t load it and schedule it to run so it finishes right when you get home from work.

This GE model features app support, allowing you to start, stop, and monitor cycles from your phone. It can also send you notifications when a load finishes and download extra wash cycles that weren’t on the machine when you bought it. It works with Alexa and Google Assistant too, so you can check on a load with just your voice.

The drum is a spacious 5.0 cubic feet with an impeller instead of an agitator, so there’s more room for bulky items. Antimicrobial protection is built into the tub cover, dispenser drawer, and drain hose to help keep mildew and odor from building up between washes. There’s a sanitize cycle too, while the dispenser has separate slots for liquid detergent, detergent pods, fabric softener, and bleach.

There is no steam option and the agitator isn’t as tough on stains, but the GE is a great option if you’re looking for smart features.

When shopping for a cheap washing machine, you’ll need to decide whether you want a full-size, portable, or manual model. Most of the full-size options you’ll find under $1,000 are top-loading washers, and they offer a large capacity as well as more settings and cycles. However, there are a few select front-loading models in this price range, as well.

For those with limited space, portable washing machines have a more compact footprint and can easily be stored in a closet. However, these machines typically require a faucet connection for operation and don’t always wring out your clothes, making them trickier to dry.

Finally, manual washing machines are the most affordable, but they require a bit of elbow grease for operation. You usually have to crank or agitate the machine by hand, but these models don’t require electricity, making them ideal for camping or off-the-grid living.

The capacity of washing machines is generally measured in cubic feet. Most standard-size appliances have a capacity of 3.5 to 5 cubic feet and are suitable for average households. For reference, a washer with a capacity of 4.5 cubic feet can wash a king-size comforter. If you have a small household, you’ll likely be fine with a smaller-capacity washing machine. A compact machine with 2.3 cubic feet can wash about 6 towels.

Cheap washing machines often have fewer wash cycles than more expensive models. In general, you’ll find most affordable washers have between eight and 12 wash cycles, including standard ones like quick or light wash, delicates, and heavy-duty. There are also several temperature settings on most washers, and some allow you to select the water level and soil level as well. These basics are generally sufficient for most loads of laundry, but if you want more advanced settings—such as sanitization or fabric-specific cycles—you may need to spend a little extra.

To help save money on operation costs, you may want to look for a high-efficiency washing machine, frequently abbreviated as HE. These models use 20 to 66 percent less water, saving around 6,000 gallons of water per year for an average family. You may also want to look for an Energy Star-certified appliance, which uses 25 percent less energy than standard models.

Amy Chernoff, VP of Marketing and Appliance Expert at AJ Madison, says that budget washing machines will still get the job done. The differences are in everything else—build quality, noise, fabric care, and how long the machine holds up under heavy use.

The trade-offs at lower price points are less about cleaning power and more about small details. “You are usually giving up fabric care refinement and overall build quality rather than basic cleaning performance,” Chernoff says.

That means simpler drum movement, fewer specialty cycles, and suspension systems that don’t dampen vibration as well. Over the years, a pricier washer tends to be gentler on your clothes, but for most people washing everyday loads, a more affordable model gets the job done.

A cheap washer doesn’t automatically mean higher utility bills. “Many affordable modern models are still quite efficient, especially if they carry an Energy Star certification,” Chernoff says. Some of the machines on this list are Energy Star certified, so they should be just as efficient as more expensive models.

A single person or couple can usually get by with 3.5 to 4.5 cubic feet. Families should look at 4.5 cubic feet or larger, which offers enough room for bedding, towels, and several days of clothes in one load.

“Choosing a slightly larger machine than you think you need can reduce the number of loads per week and make laundry more convenient over time,” Chernoff says. Every washer on this list falls between 4.2 and 5.0 cubic feet, so even the smallest option here handles a full week of laundry for two people without cramming everything in.

#6252. Crocodiles face a hidden threat that may weaken a vital survival response

Caimans with more mercury in their blood showed a weaker stress hormone response, raising concerns about how pollution affects their survival.

Mercury pollution may be weakening the stress response in crocodiles and their relatives.

Researchers studying smooth-fronted caimans in South American rainforests found that animals with more mercury in their blood had a weaker stress hormone response.

Gold mining is a major source of mercury pollution in South America. The findings suggest that mercury may interfere with a natural defense system that caimans and other crocodilians depend on to survive in the wild.

Jérémy Lemaire of the University of Vienna led the project with colleagues there and at the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna.

The researchers studied 20 adult and nearly adult caimans in French Guiana between November 2023 and June 2024.

“Given the overlap of crocodylian habitats with gold mining activities, this is a conservation concern that deserves immediate attention,” Lemaire said.

Since the late 1800s, atmospheric mercury has risen an estimated 300% to 500% above its natural level, mostly from burning fossil fuels.

Small-scale gold mining is a major contributor to this pollution. It produces 38% of the mercury released into the air worldwide, and more than 80% of mercury emissions in South America and sub-Saharan Africa combined.

Caimans live a long time and take in mercury mainly through their food. Over many years, it builds up in their bodies, which makes them a useful measure of how polluted their streams and forests are.

The authors describe mercury as an endocrine-disrupting chemical, meaning one that interferes with the body’s hormones.

Theirs is the first study to measure this hormone response in wild animals living in a tropical forest with high mercury levels, the team wrote.

The researchers studied caimans in different parts of the rainforest. One of the sites was the Nouragues nature reserve.

They caught the animals between 8 and 11 p.m. to account for the natural changes in stress hormone levels throughout the day.

Researchers caught each caiman with a snare pole. They taped its snout shut and laid a wet towel over its eyes, so every animal went through the same experience.

Then they drew blood four times. The first sample came within 3 to 5 minutes of capture to estimate baseline hormone levels. The rest came 15, 30, and 60 minutes after capture.

Red blood cells went to the mercury test. The liquid part of the blood went to a test for corticosterone, the main stress hormone in reptiles and birds.

Mercury in the caimans’ dried red blood cells ranged from about 0.3 to 2 parts per million. The team split the animals into three groups: four with low levels, nine in the middle, and seven with high levels.

At the first blood draw, resting hormone levels were about the same in all three groups. The groups differed only in the one-hour sample.

In the low and middle groups, hormone levels rose over the hour. In the high-mercury group, the levels didn’t change by a statistically significant amount at any point.

At 60 minutes, the high group’s levels were lower than those of both other groups. The high-mercury caimans started with similar hormone levels but showed a smaller increase after capture.

Across all 20 animals, the more mercury a caiman carried, the smaller the difference between its resting level and its level at one hour. Mercury levels accounted for about 40% of the variation in that difference.

The most contaminated caiman’s hormone increase was more than 100 times smaller than that of the least contaminated one.

“A fast, robust stress response is essential for survival in the wild,” Lemaire said.

“We show that even relatively low mercury burdens affect this response in caimans, potentially limiting their ability to cope with predators, extreme weather, human disturbance, and ultimately survive in the wild.”

Stress hormones work by attaching to a protein called the glucocorticoid receptor, which helps activate the body’s stress response.

Mercury can interfere with this process. Studies in male rats found that mercury made it harder for hormones to attach to the receptor.

Computer simulations also suggest that mercury can partly block the hormone’s binding site by attaching to an amino acid called cysteine.

Lemaire’s team found this same amino acid in the receptors of crocodilians and other vertebrates. This could help explain their findings, although they haven’t tested the effect directly in caiman cells.

The caimans had mercury levels similar to those found in other crocodilians worldwide.

Some slender-snouted crocodiles in Gabon, for example, have had blood mercury levels as high as 11 parts per million.

The researchers say the problem may extend beyond areas near gold mines. Even at the levels found in this study, mercury was linked to a weaker stress response.

More than a third of the 26 living crocodilian species are threatened with extinction, according to the IUCN.

Mercury pollution could put them at greater risk if it affects their ability to survive and reproduce.

The effects on wild populations could take years to become noticeable.

Since the late 1800s, crocodilians have gone through about five generations. In comparison, large land animals with generations lasting 5 to 10 years have gone through around 20.

Crocodilians take a long time to produce new generations, which can make changes in their populations difficult to detect.

Researchers still need to find out whether caimans with weaker stress responses are more likely to die or have fewer offspring.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.
