#6237. The 8 Best Space Heaters to Keep the Chill Out of Your Home and Office

We compared different models’ heating levels, timer functions, safety features, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Take the edge off those chilly winter nights without ballooning your energy bill. Space heaters offer immediate warmth for cozy nights in the bedroom and for brisk days in a drafty office. The small radius of heat also makes them ideal for improving the temperature in your immediate surroundings without wasting energy turning up the thermostat and heating the entire house. Some even double as fans during the summer.

The top space heaters run quietly and efficiently, offer multiple heating levels, and come with safety features like automatic shut-off for accidental tipping. We researched and tested the most promising models from brands like Vornado, Lasko, and Dreo. Below, you’ll find our selections for the most efficient, durable, and safest space heaters out there.

We tested space heaters by first evaluating each model based on important factors like safety, setting variety, and size. We paid attention to how well the appliances were able to warm up a space by using them around our homes and offices. We also took note of the number of heat settings each unit had and the temperature range they offered.

To evaluate the unit’s heat capabilities, we took into account its temperature range and wattage, and prioritized heaters that offered a broad range with good control and output of at least 1,200 watts or more. We’ve made a point to include options that operate via remote-controlled desktops and smart picks that come with a companion app as well.

For heaters that we haven’t had the chance to try in person, we heavily vetted specs and assessed each space heater based on the same factors we used during testing.

Lasko calls the CW100 bladeless because it doesn’t technically have a fan, per se. Instead, it uses a multi-vane impeller. That design contributes to the appliance’s quiet operation because it pulls in air through its base and into the tower. It comes with a cleanable air filter, which is accessible via a tool-free hatch at the back of the heater—no tools required.

We appreciate the slick touchpad on the front for adjusting the wattage for the heating element, tower oscillation, and the eight-hour timer. The space heater only has two actual heat settings—high and low—but there is a manual thermostat for controlling temperatures, which helps make up for the lack of power options.

The wide window of airflow and consistent heat distribution helps bring a room up to temp faster than most space heaters on this list, and this unit covers up to 300 square feet. One gripe: The battery hatch cover on the remote is tricky to remove. There is a holster for that remote control, though, making for one tidy package.

Full Lasko Oscillating Bladeless Ceramic Tower Space Heater Review

For a low-cost option, the Vornado MVH Vortex Heater heats a surprisingly large area—up to 256 square feet—with minimal noise. This unit worked well in a bedroom that has exterior walls on five sides, even during cold overnight temperatures. We like how simple, compact, and lightweight this unit is, and the appliance case stays cool to the touch, so you can move it around safely without concern.

The unit’s controls are a miss for us, though. While we liked the simple on/off button and the three-position toggle for heat levels, the thermostat dial is vague. The numbers on this dial range from 1 to 7, which don’t really show how warm each setting is.

As a result, we had to experiment with different settings until we figured out what worked best for us (you’ll likely have to do the same). Despite this drawback, the thermostat feature is helpful for when temperatures dip or get too high, as it manages the unit’s auto shutoff/on feature.

Full Vornado MVH Vortex Space Heater Review

It’s rare to come across a space heater that oscillates both horizontally and vertically, and that’s the feature we liked the most while testing the Dreo Whole Room Heater. It rotates 60 degrees up and down and 90 degrees from side to side for noticeably more coverage. Better yet, you can use both oscillation modes at the same time.

This space heater also has three heat and fan settings, and we appreciated being able to control the fan speed separately, even if we were running on high heat. Temperatures range from 41 to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, so we were able to truly customize the output. We kept our space heater at 73°F a majority of the time, and we never felt overheated or chilly.

The space heater comes with a remote, but there’s also a control panel on the base of the unit. The main thing we don’t like is that the remote was a little confusing to navigate at first. You have to use one button to access the fan speeds, heat levels, and temperatures, so we found ourselves clicking through a few times to get to the setting we wanted.

If your office is generally cold, then a heater small enough to sit on your desk might be the perfect solution for dealing with the frigid temperatures of your building. At only 12 inches tall, the Ellipse ceramic heater from Lasko is truly a compact model— discreet enough to tuck into the corner or underneath a workspace.

The highest settings pump out powerful heat in seconds, but there are medium and low settings if you want toned-down warmth. Temperatures are adjustable through the touch panel on the space heater.

We appreciate that even though this is a smaller design, it comes with its own remote. You can make the space heater oscillate and conveniently set a timer with the press of a couple buttons, and everything is viewable from the LED panel on the front.

The only thing we didn’t particularly like is that the Ellipse turns on at the highest setting automatically, so you’ll have to make adjustments almost immediately to find the ideal temperature and power.

A tech-facing space heater certainly has its benefits. The Lasko Therma-Smart tower heater has WiFi connectivity and pairs with the Aria home app for a virtual remote.

Connecting the heater was fairly easy: simply hold the WiFi button on the space heater for five seconds so it enters “pairing mode,” and then connect the device to the app. You can see wattage use and heat levels, and there’s a temperature dial in the center of the page to adjust to your liking. The Therma-Smart heater also pairs with Google and Alexa if you prefer to use voice commands.

Otherwise, the space heater has similar settings to other Lasko models that we recommend, like touch-sense controls and a digital window for viewing purposes. There are low, medium, and high heat settings, a max heat output of 1,500 watts, and a 12-hour timer function for running most of the day. One thing we noticed is that the oscillating feature seems to move very slowly, so you still might get hit with targeted heat if you’re sitting directly in front of the heater before it starts the rotation again.

The Lasko 751320 Ceramic Tower Heater is a reliable, mid-range option for homes and offices. Tester and Popular Mechanics editor Tom Price loves this model for its versatility. “The tower design and mid-sized build mean you can comfortably place it on a coffee table in the living room without it taking over the space. At the same time, it isn’t so small that I don’t feel the heat in larger spaces.”

The space heater has programmable controls that will turn the unit off and on after a certain period of time (or once the room has reached the desired temperature). It’s also equipped with an oscillating mode and comes with a multi-functioning remote control, too.

Although the gate on the front of the heater is designed to be cool to the touch, one aspect to keep in mind is that this unit does not come with an auto shutoff feature in case it gets tipped over.

A cold bathroom early in the morning feels like punishment, but a space heater on the floor near a bathtub or shower isn’t exactly a safe alternative. This fixed, wall-mounted unit from Dreo is a more reliable alternative. It’s IP24 waterproof-rated, so it’s protected against splashes from every direction, and has the same kind of ALCI plug you typically find on hair tools.

The bathroom heater accommodates spaces up to 200 square feet. With smart functionality, the companion app allows you to schedule timers, adjust temperatures, and change heat levels remotely.

Though this model has a child lock and a cool-touch exterior, we recommend mounting it out of reach of littles because the exhaust vent gets pretty warm.

If noise is one of your biggest concerns while shopping for a space heater, then an oil-filled radiator heater might be the right option. The Pelonis heater doesn’t use an internal fan, and offers the quietest noise operation on our list, maxing out right around five decibels.

It offers just about the same features as the ceramic heaters we recommend, with three different heating modes, tip-over security, and overheat protection. The heater has 360-degree warmth circulation, so you’re covered from every angle.

The radiator sits on four casters so it easily moves from room to room. It has a carrying handle, but it’s relatively small compared to the overall size of the unit and may overheat, so we recommend moving to your desired space before turning it on.

Simple, affordable, and versatile, these use electrical resistance to warm your space. A ceramic block or element is electrically conductive and heats up, and that heat is transferred to the air with an internal fan. The majority of the heaters on our list fall into this category.

Ideal use: These are great for general household use, shared offices, or wherever quiet heat is needed. Their simplicity makes them quite rugged; they have fewer parts to wear out or break.

This style of space heater emits infrared radiation rays that heat objects and individuals rather than the air, and it’s one of the more straightforward designs. They provide warmth almost instantly and aren’t loud while running, but they do have limited range.

Ideal use: Spot heating or small areas that need to be warmed up in a short amount of time.

These appliances burn propane or kerosene to warm an infrared emitter that projects the energy to heat your space. They’re considered convection heaters because they transfer thermal energy through a fluid, either by gas or oil.

They elevate the temperature of the air in certain spaces and are most suitable for delivering warmth in an area where you might walk around, like the surroundings of your desk or workshop.

Ideal use: Construction sites, garages, or work areas are the best places to use these heaters, since you want to place one at a comfortable distance and keep the work area unobstructed. Gas or liquid-fuel heaters direct the heat wherever you’re working.

Most residential space heaters use about 1,500 watts of power. If you’re using one of these devices as a primary heat source, it’s recommended to choose a model that offers 10 watts of heat output per square foot of space. 150 square feet is the common standard for coverage. You may consider investing in more than one unit if you’re trying to warm a larger space, or finding a design that has the right power combined with a fan or oscillating mode to disperse heat more evenly.

If you have pets or young children, then choosing a space heater with safety features is especially important for avoiding accidental burns and fires. The majority of the heaters on our list come with an automatic shut-off feature if it tips over. A good portion of our recommended heaters also include a timer to prevent the device from running for the entire day if you forget to shut it off.

During our testing and research journey, we learned some other valuable safety tips along the way such as the “three feet rule” (keeping the space heater at a distance from anything flammable) and not using these appliances in moist areas. But most importantly, you should never plug a space heater into an extension cord, power cord, or power strip. They’re not equipped for the electrical load that these devices require, and can be a potential fire hazard.

The short answer is it depends. Whether it’s “a lot” depends mainly on how long you run the heater and your local electricity rate. In the U.S., residential electricity prices typically range from $0.12 to $0.20 per kWh, with the average being around $0.17 per kWh as of December 2025.

Because most space heaters operate at 1,500 watts, they can cost between $0.18 and $0.30 per hour at average electricity rates. To find a more accurate estimate, divide the heater’s wattage by 1,000 to convert to kilowatts, then multiply that number by the number of hours the heater is running, and multiply that result by your electricity rate per kilowatt-hour (kWh).

These appliances aren’t intended to replace your home’s central heating system, so it’s better to use them supplementally if you don’t want to pay more on your electric bill.

You should turn them off when sleeping or left unattended. Common overnight hazards like a unit tipping over, bedding sitting too close to the heater, or an outlet overheating pose significant risks that you might not notice until you wake up. While most space heaters have preventative safety features like automatic shutoff or built-in thermostats, and may even be rated for continuous use, it’s best to resist the temptation of 24-hour warmth for safer operation.

#6236. Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Michigan woman uses a brain implant to speak with her neurosurgeon. Efforts to restore speech highlight what’s at stake when we lose opportunities to talk.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.

“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”

Laura Sanders: OK, I want to ask who your favorite comedians are and why. Who makes you all laugh?

Jules Rodriguez: Pete Holmes and Mike Birbiglia are some of my favorites.

[Audio] He was just like, I’m a bear, et cetera.

[Audio] The best part of sleep is falling asleep. That’s the only part you’re there for.Jules: Their styles are different, but I have always gravitated towards their authenticity.

Sanders: There’s another comedian who is extra meaningful for Jules: Conan O’Brien.

[Audio] Today is a bit of a different sort of episode. I’ll be talking to Jules and Maria.

Sanders: After MA had reached out, Conan invited the couple onto his podcast, where they connected about comedy. Conan still checks in on Jules every so often.

[Audio] It’s incredible to me that in our conversations, you’re very frank about the pain that you go through, and how intense it is. But you’re also always so positive and funny and, frankly, you give me a lot of [beep]. Which I find to be, well I hate it, by the way, first of all. Oh, get over it, Conan.

Jules: Conan is very special to me. Watching and listening to him helped me disconnect from the harsh reality of my life. And when I got to meet him and chat with him, it meant the world to me.

Maria Aleandra Fernandez: Having the most normal conversation with Conan O’Brien is something I will never get over.

[Audio] So he has a bunch of banked phrases. He’s going to play a few of our favorites. OK. I’m fine. I’m perfectly [beep] fine. [laughter] Come on man, are we doing this or not? Oh my God, oh my God. I’m destroying this marriage. MA: He really is so genuine and like, not only willing to talk to us, but really looks forward to talking. Like, I love talking to you guys. I’m not just doing it to be a nice person, which feels, you know, feels wonderful.

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.

Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.

MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle. [Audio] Dave Chappelle says he is very clear about his role as a comedian.

MA: And Dave Chappelle said something that is so spot-on. He said that comedians are how people metabolize things.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.

MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.

It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. It just disarms everything. You’re just like, oh, OK. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.

Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

By using their voices, by telling their stories, by telling their jokes, Jules and MA are helping me, and maybe you too, metabolize the pain – and the joy – of living. Welcome to The Deep End, Talk to Me.

[Voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.

Sanders: I’m Laura Sanders and today, we’re going to look ahead to what’s coming next for the human voice and efforts to restore it.

Sanders: In some ways, this podcast is a story of progress, of figuring out, little by little, more about the brain, and more about technology and more about people. Today, Jules can type with his eyes, and his son can hear his dad’s voice say I love you. In earlier episodes, you heard from Casey Harrell. Casey can think about saying a word to his daughter, and boom, they’re off playing a game together.

Casey Harrell: So this has kept me still in touch with people and the world, and it is not hyperbole to frame it this way.

Sanders: Paradromics has developed its own brain-computer interface for communication. The device is about the size of a dime, and it sits on the motor cortex. That’s the part of the brain that creates speech signals. The chip then detects these signals as a person thinks about saying a word.

Matthew Willsey: So the cortical module has 421 tiny little sensors.

Sanders: That’s neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer Matthew Willsey, of the University of Michigan Health. He’s describing the device from Paradromics here.

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Sanders: Those tiny sensors are listening to the nearby neurons that control the muscles required for speech.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6235. You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims

What if growing up makes you more knowledgeable but less aware of reality?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

It sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that currently exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

Muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

Muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

In preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he says. “It’s very new, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”

Muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he says. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

He thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

“It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

However, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik says.

Muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

For now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

Stav Dimitropoulos is a Gold and Community Anthem Award–winning journalist, and writes about consciousness, science, and culture for Popular Mechanics, Nature, and the BBC. Her work often explores mind-stretching angles where science meets philosophy. Her debut nonfiction book, Slow, Lazy, Gluttons (Greystone Books, 2026) asks: What if the traits society shames — laziness, darkness, nostalgia, and more — are actually survival superpowers?

#6234. When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds

You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind. On a first visit, you want time to take in the massive scale of the Inca city on its forested ridge above the Urubamba River, and then to walk among its stone walls. That picture, of course, depends on the weather. Here, where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, a single bank of cloud can hide Waynapicchu, the peak behind the ruins, and with it the panorama you came to see.

The drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours. The weeks just after the rains offer greener slopes—and often thinner crowds—to anyone prepared to pack for showers. The best time to visit Machu Picchu comes down to matching the conditions to the type of visit you want, as well as confirming that your route is available before you commit to booking trains and rooms. Below are the questions that first-time visitors ask most, with advice from travel advisors and experts.

For a first visit, May and September—before and after the June-to-August rush, respectively—will have generally favorable walking weather, before the rains creep back in October. The two months aren’t interchangeable, especially if you hope to walk to the Sun Gate or the Inca Bridge. The 2026 route calendar opened those seasonal paths in September but not in May, so check the 2027 dates as soon as they’re published.

April brings greener slopes to anyone who can live with a little more water. “It’s also shoulder season so there aren’t many tourists yet,” says Alice Farkas, who leads marketing and communications at Aracari, a company based in Lima that plans private trips across South America. Kiernan Cochran, product manager at Andean, which plans trips throughout Peru, also favors April into early May. Even so, Cochran’s team books those weeks for travelers with much the same lead time as high season, since popular routes fill early.

When it comes to visiting Machu Picchu, daily timing might matter even more than which time of year you visit.

November through March offers significant savings on airfare and accommodations, though strategic planning remains essential. Permits for popular routes like Huayna Picchu still require three-month advance booking during these months (compared to six months of required lead time during peak season).

Mosquera makes a case for embracing the rainy season: "It's actually my favorite time. The site becomes magical with fewer crowds given that overtourism is one of Machu Picchu's greatest threats. The rain isn't nearly as disruptive as people imagine, as it mainly falls in the evenings, not all day. February is particularly special because the Inca Trail closes for maintenance, making the site even quieter." (Note: If you plan to arrive by trek, options will be more limited during these moments.)

The wet season transforms the landscape dramatically. Stone terraces flush vibrant green, hidden waterfalls emerge, and morning mist creates atmospheric reveals of the citadel. The timing also aligns perfectly with Peru's coastal summer. "More travelers are discovering this split-season strategy," says Mosquera. "You can explore misty ruins early in the trip, then travel down to Lima's world-class restaurants or Máncora's beaches where summer's in full swing." Temperatures at Machu Picchu remain moderate year-round, with rain typically following predictable afternoon patterns rather than all-day downpours.

The dry months from June through August draw the main crush of tourists, when the most desirable entry hours can sell out along with hotels and trains. Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun, culminates in Cusco on June 24, and Peru’s Independence Day on July 28 brings another surge. In 2026, the daily cap was 4,500 visitors on ordinary dates and 5,600 on specified days, including June 19 through November 2, though that calendar doesn’t automatically carry over to 2027. Those places are also divided by route and hour, so your preferred route and entry time may be full even when the site has space overall.

Once each year’s tickets are released, Andean suggests booking sought-after routes about six months ahead in high season and at least three months ahead in low season.

Allow four or five nights in the region, as Cochran recommends, and begin in the Sacred Valley if your itinerary allows. Its Inca towns and terraces also mean the citadel isn’t your first encounter with the culture that built it. Cusco, where flights land for now, sits at roughly 11,150 feet. Heading straight down to the valley gives you a gentler start, and you can return to explore the city afterward. Cusco’s long-delayed replacement airport, Chinchero International, is under construction on the plateau above the Sacred Valley at about 12,340 feet, higher than the city itself. Its opening is targeted for late 2027, so most 2027 trips will still begin at the old one.

Ollantaytambo, at about 9,160 feet, is halfway between Cusco and Machu Picchu, and where travelers board the train to the latter. The town of ‘Ollanta’ has Inca-era streets and archaeological sites to explore, and is well worth a stop either going to or coming from Machu Picchu (the lovely El Albergue hotel sits just beside the train station).

From there, travelers catch the train to Aguas Calientes, also known as Machu Picchu Pueblo, which is the small town at the base of the ancient citadel. Spend the night prior to your Machu Picchu visit in Aguas Calientes for an early start up the mountain. Some allow just one day at Machu Picchu; others who want to appreciate the landmark from a few perspectives should budget two. You may, for instance, want to experience an upper terrace or a mountain climb alongside Classic Circuit 2, which is the standard walk through the Inca city (more on these routes below). If so, book that second route for another day. Either way, you can usually spend a full day at Machu Picchu and still catch a late afternoon/early evening train out, or bed down for another night in Aguas Calientes and depart the next morning.

Before buying anything sold simply as “Machu Picchu admission,” take a look at the official route maps, since the three circuits divide the site by elevation and access. For a single visit, Andean favors Classic Circuit 2. Its routes 2-A and 2-B each pair a viewpoint with a walk among the Inca buildings of the urban sector. Route 2-B takes its view from the lower terrace, a distinction worth knowing if you have a particular camera angle in mind.

For the upper-terrace panorama, choose Circuit 1’s route 1-B, which keeps you above the main streets, while route 1-A adds the climb up Machu Picchu Mountain which offers the classic view down onto the site. The Sun Gate and Inca Bridge carry seasonal tickets of their own. Circuit 3 covers the lower royal sector, including the Temple of the Sun. Its route 3-A adds the steep ascent of Waynapicchu (often spelled Huayna Picchu), which is the distinctive peak in the background of most Machu Picchu photos, and 3-B stays below. If Circuit 2 sells out, Andean suggests booking Circuits 1 and 3 separately to combine the panorama with a closer look at the ruins. Choose wisely before you arrive, since a ticket cannot be switched to another route at the gate.

Hikers face their own paperwork. Permits for the classic Inca Trail are limited and booked through authorized operators, and the shorter one-day trail from kilometer 104 of the rail line needs a permit and an operator, too. That day hike is Cochran’s own favorite—the final leg of the historic Inca route to the Sun Gate, without the multiday inn-to-inn or camping journey required. Ask what your hike covers before buying a separate admission.

Under the September 2026 rules, trail arrivals enter on a designated Circuit 3-B ticket, which matters if you also want Circuit 2 or the upper panorama. Heavy rain can also shut the kilometer 104 path outside the usual February maintenance period, which is something to keep in mind for any rainy season travel.

Your train booking does not include admission (treks are on a case-by-case basis; ask!), so buy entry through the Ministry of Culture’s Tu Boleto portal, where you choose your route first and your entry hour second. Enter each visitor’s details carefully, matching names and information to the same identification document they’ll present at the gate. The ticket fixes the holder’s name, date, time, and route; current rules allow no changes to the name or date after purchase.

The purchase process changed in September 2026, when the ministry began a 30-day trial of direct paid checkout in place of the earlier unpaid hold. Under the portal’s current purchase manual, you have 15 minutes from the start of an order to enter everyone’s details and pay. Have documents and payment ready, and follow the instructions on screen. Rail and admission are also released on separate timelines. PeruRail opened 2027 train sales on September 22, but Yuriko Aquino of PROMPERÚ, Peru’s tourism promotion agency, says the Ministry of Culture has yet to announce when 2027 admission will go on sale or what the daily visitor cap will be. If you buy rail first, read the fare’s change terms before you pay.

Within the overall cap, up to 1,000 tickets a day are held for in-person sale in Machu Picchu Pueblo, valid for entry the following day. If you’re counting on that uncertain fallback, budget a night in town. Whichever way you buy, a guide is recommended for a standard citadel visit, while Inca Trail hikers follow their operator’s separate requirements. Guides can be booked through your hotel or at the entrance to the site.

From Cusco, most travelers cross the Sacred Valley by road to Ollantaytambo and board the train there for the ride along the Urubamba to Machu Picchu Pueblo. From town, a separate shuttle bus climbs to the entrance in roughly half an hour. Check boarding points and total travel time before choosing a fare, since PeruRail’s January-to-April departures from Cusco involve a bus-and-train transfer.

For a first visit, Cochran favors a morning train from the Sacred Valley and an afternoon Circuit 2 entry, when her team generally finds the site less crowded; three or four hours is usually enough to take it in. Among the premium trains, she points to Belmond’s Hiram Bingham, PeruRail’s Vistadome Observatory, and IncaRail’s First Class.

Whichever train you choose, leave a cushion between arrival and admission. Peru’s tourism authority advises reaching the shuttle station about an hour before your gate slot, or setting out about two hours ahead if you plan to walk uphill. A train that pulls in just before your entry time leaves little margin for the bus queue and the gate check.

Down in Machu Picchu Pueblo are two fantastic Peruvian-owned options—Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel, with scattered adobe casitas among orchids, and Sumaq Machu Picchu Hotel, which faces the Urubamba River. Both are close to the shuttle stop. Sanctuary Lodge, a Belmond Hotel, is the only property up on the mountain at the gates of Machu Picchu, which spares you the morning shuttle ascent, though hotel guests still enter on the same timed admission as everyone else.

#6233. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6231. GLP-1s Extend Life Span, New Research Suggests. Could They Be Key to Human Longevity?

This may mean the drug also has benefits outside of diabetes management.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Roughly 11 percent of American adults are on a GLP-1 for weight loss, according to a 2026 Gallup survey; so chances are, you likely know someone who is using one for diabetes management, obesity treatment, or heart health—but the benefits might not stop there. Now, semaglutide, the popular GLP-1 medication found in Ozempic and Wegovy, is drawing serious attention from longevity experts.

A recent study published in Nature found that semaglutide administered to female mice late in life significantly extended their life span. The results pose a legitimate question: Could GLP-1 drugs lengthen human lives as well?

To understand whether GLP-1s have anti-aging benefits, researchers put mice that were 20 months old—or roughly 60 human years—on a semaglutide regimen for the rest of their lives. There was also a control group of female mice the same age that received saline injections instead of the semaglutide. The team targeted older, non-obese, non-diabetic female mice to minimize the effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term aging research, according to study author Danica Chen, PhD, professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at the University of California, Berkeley.The results? The median life span of the mice that received the GLP-1 drug increased from 742 days to 834 days, roughly a 12 percent extension. The researchers also saw reduced inflammation and preserved cognitive and muscle function in the GLP-1 group.

But there’s a rub here: This study was done in mice, which are a far cry from human adults, meaning we don’t yet know the effects of GLP-1s on people—at least not yet. However, there has been research that suggests lower-calorie diets lead to longer life spans in humans. “The general cause of aging is accumulation of cellular damage,” Chen says. She explains that calorie restriction can reduce cell damage and improve the function of tissues (a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific task), both of which contribute to a longer life span.

Michael Corley, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, thinks the Nature study is “important and exciting” because it looks beyond the established metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs and tests whether they can influence the biological aging process. (Biological age denotes how well the body is functioning on cellular and molecular levels, while chronological age refers to the number of years a person has been alive.)

“The finding that semaglutide extended life span by approximately 12 percent in older female mice, while improving several measures of physical and cognitive function, adds important evidence to the emerging field of GLP-1 therapies as potential gerotherapeutics,” or treatments that target the root of aging, Corley says. In fact, Corley was involved in a separate study, published earlier this year in Nature Communications, that found that 32 weeks of semaglutide treatment improved multiple epigenetic aging clocks, including measures of biological age and the pace of aging.

Findings presented at the 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery Meeting have also strengthened this emerging picture, Corley explains. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical company with locations around the world, reported that semaglutide improved measures of biological aging across multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys.

Likewise, Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical company headquartered in Indiana, presented findings that tirzepatide—another GLP-1 medication, which is found in prescriptions like Mounjaro and Zepbound—positively influenced several epigenetic aging clocks, including organ-specific markers that measure the biological age of the heart, kidney, liver, and immune system.

“Together, these independent observations suggest that GLP-1-based therapies may affect biological aging through multiple molecular pathways,” Corley says. “The new mouse study is particularly interesting because it extends these molecular observations to actual life span, while also demonstrating improvements in several hallmarks of aging.”

So, could GLP-1 drugs actually extend the life span of humans? Corley thinks the more compelling opportunity isn’t necessarily extending life span, but extending health span—or the number of years people live in good health, free from chronic disease and disability.

“Human life span has biological constraints, and it is unlikely that GLP-1 drugs alone will dramatically extend the maximum limits of human longevity,” he says. “However, by reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and other age-related conditions, these medications could help more people remain healthy and independent for longer, potentially increasing average life span without fundamentally changing the upper limits of human longevity.”

However, improvements in biological aging don’t necessarily translate into longer lives, Corley cautions.

“The critical next step is determining whether these molecular changes predict meaningful improvements in physical function, cognition, and resilience,” Corley says. “I think the greatest potential of GLP-1 therapies is not to push humans beyond the limits of longevity, but to help more people reach older ages while maintaining their health, function, and independence.”

To find out whether or not GLP-1 drugs can eventually be used as a legitimate longevity tactic in humans, Chen says clinical trials in humans are an important next step. For now, GLP-1s remain a titan of diabetes and weight management—but their role in human longevity remains to be seen.

#6230. Nov. 12, 2014: The Philae lander touches down on a comet

The European Space Agency’s Rosetta mission launched March 2, 2004, on a 4-billion-mile (6.4 billion kilometers) path to Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The mission consisted of the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander, both designed for in-depth study of the comet. The spacecraft arrived at 67P/C-G on Aug. 6, 2014, and began orbiting the body a month later; on Nov. 12, 2014, the Philae lander descended to the comet surface. Both the spacecraft orbiting a comet and the landing on the comet’s surface were firsts in space exploration history.

Unfortunately, there were some complications with the landing: The harpoon system that was designed to hold the lander in place didn’t work, causing Philae to bounce and to float and drift above the surface. When it finally came to rest, it was in a shadowy location now known as Abydos, limiting to the sunlight its solar panels received.

Despite these challenges, Philae was able to operate for three days on battery power, and still sent back photos and data about the composition of the comet’s dust and its analysis of the body’s magnetism. (In short, the comet didn’t have a magnetic field.) Additionally, the orbiter transmitted data about water and oxygen in the tail that led to new understanding of such comets’ makeup.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.
